utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Jim Cowles, representing the Prosecution. With me is Mr. George Huber. I need to inform the Court that Ms. McHenry experienced a death in the family and had to return home for an emergency basis. So she'll be absent from the Court for several days, so I will be representing the Prosecution, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. The Trial Chamber expresses a lot of sympathy for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Eugene O'Sullivan, and I appear on behalf of Mr. Delalic my co-counsel and lead counsel, Ms. Residovic, will be absent this morning. I would also like to introduce the presence of our legal counsel this morning, Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Zeljko Olujic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Djuric, both of us are attorneys from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic, I am an attorney from Sarajevo, and along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas, I appear on behalf of Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Cynthia McMurrey, I represent Esad Landzo. Ms. Boler will be absent from the courtroom today and Mr. Calvin Saunders will be joining me as a second attorney on the case today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. McMurrey. May we proceed now? Call your first witness. Can you swear the witness, please. Swear the witness so she might proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence calls Marco Laggazi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I will interpret independently, impartially and with full respect with the duty of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Lagazzi. Will you please introduce yourself to the Court so they know your full name.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: My name is Marco Lagazzi, forensic psychiatrist, from the Genoa University, Italy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, we met for the first time last month in June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And how did you come to be a part of this Tribunal, this International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I was first asked by the register's office to work for the Tribunal at the request of the Prosecutor, Mr. Turone, for the first inquiry on examination of Mr. Landzo, which took place in November, 1996. And there was a three-person panel, Dr. Van Leuween and Dr. Loga that worked with me on that panel. I then took another assignment in January, 1997, together with the same colleagues. In April, 1998, I was asked by the Defence counsel to again examine Mr. Landzo at the request of the counsel for the defence and notified the Tribunal about that. And in May, 1998, I was granted authorisation from the Prosecutor to carry out such an examination, was retaining my status as neutral expert, as an expert called upon by the Defence counsel, I have carried out the inquiry which took place in the second half of July, 1998, and which was then completed with a written report on the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wan to make a correction, I believe that evaluation was carried out in the last half of June, 1998, instead of July.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Correct, it was the second half of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you, you wrote a letter to the registry because you wanted to make sure that it wouldn't affect your ability to remain an independent, neutral, psychiatrist in this proceeding?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, under the Italian law, a neutral adviser, consultant, designated by the Prosecutor's office, cannot carry out an evaluation for the Defence. When I was told that there wouldn't be any difficulty, that I would still retain my status as neutral expert, I could take on the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And this was further confirmed and explained to you by a telephone call from Mr. Turone?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Indeed, I received several phone calls from the Prosecutor, Mr. Turone and I did ask him to explain exactly what I was supposed to do and when I was clarified that this is what I was supposed to do, I took on this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Tribunal, the Court, what meetings you've had since you've been in The Hague this week?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I have met the Defence counsel and the panel for the Defence attorney, McMurrey, and attorney Boler. I have met you on several occasions and I have also met with the Prosecutor, Mr. Cowles and Ms. McHenry. And I have had an informal meeting with attorney, Moran, late last night. And I have discussed with them more or less my opinion on the case. Sunday, if I recall correctly, at the request of the Defence counsel, we also had a meeting with Dr. Van Leuween and Dr. Gripon, that is two experts that worked on the case. Dr. Van Leuween worked with me on previous assignments and I met the other colleague just on that last occasion. The last meeting we've had on Sunday was also attended by Dr. Verde, who testified yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, that meeting Sunday, when we met, nobody knew what the conclusion was of the other psychiatrist, whenever we met on Sunday, did they?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I was not aware of the conclusions drawn by Dr. Gripon and Dr. Van Leuween. As to the conclusions drawn by Dr. Verde, we travelled to The Hague together, so I was informed about them and they were the basis on which I wrote my report, part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So on Sunday it was the first time that it became clear to everybody that three independent psychiatrists had basically come up with the same conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning as being irrelevant. I mean, it has nothing to do with his opinion. It's as if she's trying to support his credibility before it's even been questioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that it's important for the Court to realise that each one of these independently evaluated Mr. Landzo and independently came up with their own opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you think we would not get that when they've all testified?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: There was a joint meeting on Sunday, but all of their opinions had already been confirmed and their reports before we met on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will still get that opinion after they've all testified, so you don't have to put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll move forward then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: At this point, the Defence has filed a curriculum vitae of Dr. Lagazzi before, and we just recently received the English translation, so to assist the Court when we're going through his qualifications, I would like the usher to pass out the English version of his CV. The Prosecution was just recently supplied with one of these also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are matters which you supply at the time you are nominating him and it's not necessary for you -- we would have all got it before now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We've had it in Italian, Your Honours, but we haven't had it in a version that I could read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Pass them around without bothering to explain so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, Dr. Laggazi, I am going to let you explain your qualifications, starting off with your education?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I took high school studies and then I went to the medical school, and so I am a medical doctor. I took a medical degree in 1984. I did post graduate specialisation in medical psychology until 1988. I then took a PhD in forensic psychiatry and my PhD dissertation was given in 1992. Whilst I was at the medical school, I worked with the Forensic Criminology and Psychology Department of the Medical School of Genoa, which is part of the Genoa University. And I have been working since 1986 as forensic psychiatrist. I have had several training stages in Canada and I have been working with the School of Forensic Psychiatry of Lyon, France.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That school in France, is it considered one of the foremost leading universities in behavioural sciences?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: To qualify this, I would say that it is one of the leading centres for forensic psychiatry in the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Does it specialise more in certain types of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: In my capacity of forensic psychiatrist, I deal especially with these areas, and this is also something I have been writing papers on, and I deal especially with problems dealing with mental illness, criminal behaviour, interactions between psychiatric services and Tribunals. And I do work in a number of Italian cities with Prosecutor's offices and with the law and order officials and in determining the profiles of serial killers and I work on problems concerning the perpetrators of major crimes. It is organised crime and serial killers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And what exactly is your position at the University of Genoa?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I am an Associate Professor of Forensic Psychology at the post graduate School of Criminology and Forensic Psychiatry at the Genoa University.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And has the School of Forensic Medicine in Genoa, has it changed recently to be more all encompassing?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: As I pointed out -- as was pointed out by Dr. Verde, we have been set up as a department, which covers medical psychology, forensic medicine, Criminology, and forensic psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you hold other positions at other universities, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. I do teach the same disciplines as visiting professor on short-term contracts at the Milan University, the Turin University and I teach the same disciplines and subjects in a number of schools that issue master degrees. And I have also received assignments for the training of medical staff with the Justice Department. And I am also responsible for training of judges and magistrates at the request of the higher counsel for the judiciary in Italy. And also I am in charge of training psychologically and psychiatry of various members of staff of Italian administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you work at the Department of Justice in the local administrations, do you tend to specialise more in violent behaviour?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Well, forensic psychiatry encompasses a great many aspects and not necessarily just violent behaviour. For a number of years now, I have been working especially on problems related to severe crimes, major crimes, violent behaviour, such as the behaviour of a serial killer or linked to organised crime perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what some of your scientific positions are? What boards you're a member of, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: In scientific terms, I'll try and recap my assignments and my qualifications. I am a member of the International Society for Criminology, I am a member of the Board of the Italian Academy of Psychiatry, Psychology and Law. There are eight members to this academy. I am a member of the Scientific Committee of the Italian Society of Criminology. It's a 20 person board. And I am a member of the Board of the Italian Society of Forensic Psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Dr. Lagazzi, you're also a judge in Italy, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I am an honorary judge of the so-called Tribunal, which is responsible for probation and other tasks of this nature on convicted detainees. And it's a Tribunal that is composed of two experts and two judges, two experts that are forensic psychiatrists, criminologists that serve as judges and I have been serving in this position since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also participate in military hospitals through the army in Italy, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. For a number of years, I have been in charge as a civilian, medical officer for the selection of those that wanted to join the Italian Army to evaluate their ability to be in the military, especially with respect to possible psychological problems that it might have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So when you do this clinical, psychiatric evaluation for recruitment purposes, you're specifically looking for personality disorders; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go on to another topic that you're an expert in. You've written several books, but you've also written several papers on the topic of malandering (sic) -- malingering, I'm sorry. Would you explain to the Trial Chamber what your expertise is in this area of malingering?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is, and I'll use the English term, malingering, which is something that -- something more precisely in Italian term. In Italian, we're forced to use the word simulation and dissimulation, two terms. So people who pretend to have psychological or psychiatric disorders and they try to cover them up. I have been involved with this as part of my activities on behalf of the Military Hospital. Indeed, we've carried out a study and we have published a study on the issue. And I have also written papers on this subject as well. And we have dealt with this in a number of different treatises. The last thing I wrote on this subject goes back to a forensic psychological handbook, which I carried out with a colleague from the University of Genoa, which will be published in October and where we deal exclusively with the problems of simulation and dissimulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So this is a textbook to be published in October and you wrote the chapter on malingering; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. I have written the entire book on this subject, so of course there are chapters that deal with this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Court the two different aspects of malingering. You call them simulation and dissimulation, but exactly what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that one finds not just in the military field, but, basically, in all psychiatric events. Let's just say that we often encounter this in problems found in the military sphere when your find people who don't want to do their military service, for example, and therefore they pretend to have psychological problems. And then, very often, we work for the courts who have personality disorders, people who try to simulate an attitude which is probably better than the one that they actually had. Simulation is often found in white-collar crimes and what people try to do is try to simulate a psychiatric disorder which they don't suffer from. And almost on a daily basis, in organised crime we encounter such cases, so the psychiatric symptoms, are, in fact, non-existent. Dissimulation is the opposite of this. In other words, we're dealing with people who do have psychiatric disorders, people who, to a certain extent, are aware of having such psychiatric disorders, and, therefore, this excludes the real psychotic who is not aware of his illness. And this type of person tends to hide his psychiatric disorders. In the military field, we would encounter cases where you have people in the armed forces or in the police force who have alcoholic problems and try and hide such alcoholism so that they can stay in the force. We also frequently find it in such cases where there is a person, for example, who may have senile dementia and carries out certain acts on the basis of pure pathological cause, but tries to defend what he has done, and therefore, tries to hide his own difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when someone has this dissimulation of malingering, also you're looking whether they have antisocial behaviour or schizoid or anything like that that they're hiding?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, we carry out a global psychological evaluation, so we look at pathologies, and we see whether they have psychological problems or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, would you say that Mr. Landzo suffers from both of these aspects of malingering?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: To a certain extent I would say yes. But if you want me to go into more detail, I think it would be anticipating the entire discussion, so I would prefer you to ask me that question later on, when I have expanded the results from the various observations that I have made and then I will be able to explain what are the dissimulation or simulation aspects that I have discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Dr. Lagazzi. I am still right in the middle of your qualifications. Would you explain to the Court how many expertises a year you complete or you participate in?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Well, I am talking about an average. Let's say, every year 100, 120, 130 expertises I carry out a year. But that is an expertise carried out on behalf of the courts, of course, as a court-appointed expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And going further with that, the majority of the time that you're performing expertise, you're working on behalf of the Prosecution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, let me put it this way. In many cases, I work directly as an expert appointed by the Court. But there are cases where we're dealing with serial killers and other cases involving organised crime. I work directly with the Prosecutor. But not -- and not just as a psychiatric expert to carry out an evaluation, but I also carry out the examination of the survey, so I work with the police force or the Carabinieri, which is the military police in Italy. And during the examination procedure, when we're identifying the various profiles of the criminal, and we're looking at the instruments which are most suitable in order to identify the criminal and to understand from a psychiatric and psychological perspective if the personality of the person who has been arrested is consistent with the crimes that are laid at his door. So, it is an investigative role as well that we play.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So that in the investigative role that you play, you're also trying to help them to solve the crime; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, in this part of my work, yes. I think it is right to say that in my role as an expert in forensic psychology, appointed by the court or by the Prosecutor, as part of a trial case, my role is that of a neutral expert. The other part of my work, obviously, is one that could be defined as being a psychiatric consultant appointed by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you prepared three reports dealing with Mr. Landzo and evaluating Mr. Landzo in these proceedings before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you take a look at your first report?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And would you explain to the Court the scope of this report and what it is that you determine from that evaluation of Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. I was charged on the first of November, 1996, with a task of identifying whether or not there was a psychiatric disorder, such as to prevent Mr. Landzo from participating in the trial. In other words, to determine whether he was able to participate in the trial. Discussing things with the judge who appointed me, Ms. de Sampayo from the registry office, I was asked to carry out an urgent examination of the suicide risk. In other words, the first question which I have reacted to after visiting Mr. Landzo on an emergency manner, was the measures that needed to be adopted in order to prevent any new acts of self-mutilation. And over the next two-day period we discussed things with Ms. de Sampayo and President Cassase of the most appropriate measures in and order to allow us to manage the incarceration of Mr. Landzo. I then continued the discussions in order to address the issue which was asked of me, namely to determine whether he could participate in the trial or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But at the time that you did this evaluation, you thought that the risk of suicide, was it real or not real?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I think that there was a real risk and, indeed, a high risk. And I advised that psychotherapy be used and that it be provided to Mr. Landzo. Rarely have I seen judges who are so aware of such problems. And we work together to reduce this risk, so it has been a very interesting professional experience for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In other words, this was a very caring Tribunal, who really was concerned about the life or death or risk involved with their detainees?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. In my experience, I can say categorically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just want to cover one thing, and I would like the registrar to know that I will provide them with all three copies at the next break. The only one I have in my possession right now is marked on, so -- I want to go to something that Mr. Moran talked about yesterday on cross-examination of Dr. Verde. Mr. Moran was reading a part of your report to Dr. Verde, asserting that Mr. Landzo was able to fool you regarding his malingering. Now, on page 35 of this report --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Sorry, the English version you're talking about, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am very fortunate, Your Honours, that Dr. Lagazzi does -- speaks very good English too. Now, would you further explain your findings from your November 15th report to the Trial Chamber, indicating that, of course, you recognised malingering.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I must say that it this was a simulation attempt, which was a very course indeed. I've had discussions with the gentleman in question in the beginning and, looking at a number of problems that were consistent with his personality, it was clearly a person who was capable of remembering sufficient details. They were logical details, reasoning links, which he was able to follow. Now, obviously, there was a lot of psychological suffering in all of this, but he was able to express his opinions and he was aware that an expertise was being carried out. He is aware of time and space. He was aware of the criminal proceedings being instituted against him. And then, in one single interview, the one carried out on the 15th of November, 1996, I think it was, then suddenly, during a meeting in the presence of his Defence attorney -- I say consultant because professor Loga, in fact, was a member of our group of experts, but he was designated as Defence attorney. And all of a sudden, he started the interview saying that he didn't know what the season was. He didn't know what day of the week it was. And, therefore, this type of malingering was quite evident. And in my report I have pointed this out. But I think it's quite clear that if you have a person who on the previous day is perfectly aware of time and space factors, recognise people, speaks to me and knows exactly whom I am, then we discuss things together, and the following day, changes his attitude in a way which is akin to somebody who has been subjected to a real blow, a strong blow to the head. As he didn't get such a strong blow to the head, one can assume that this is a case of malingering. These were things that were so inconsistent and so clearly inconsistent with the rest. I have pointed all this out in my report. I think it is impossible from a clinical perspective for an individual without any clinical, serious clinical effects taking place, and who on the previous day is able to reason, is able to reason, is able to talk in a logical manner, and the following day shows that he is incapacitated, that he cannot reason any more. So, that is not a real clinical case and it's quite obvious in such cases that this apparent cancellation of psychological skills, unless there is a clinical reason to explain this during the course of time, one has to assume that it is a case of malingering. Indeed, his logical reasoning capacity has always remained in tact, not perfect, but I must say that they haven't been cancelled out. Certainly not during the examination that we carried out. Sorry. And I concluded my report, pointing out that we were dealing here with a person with problem disorders. And I said that there was a symptom which was evident of a post-traumatic stress disorder. And I concluded, nevertheless, that he was quite capable of standing trial, nevertheless. So, if the affirmations that he made during that single interview regarding that he was completely disoriented and had no idea about time and space, if we had recognised that, obviously he would not have been capable of standing trial, but that was not the case. I should also like to add that I made also a recommendation here and I said that if one could have psychotherapy treatment, we could, perhaps, prevent a case of suicide.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, going back to Mr. Moran's incomplete statement yesterday, you didn't use the word, malingering in your report, but you did notify the Court that this cannot be clinically justified and it was due to lack of cooperation by the subject?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Lack of cooperation on the part of the subject is a term that is used and its somewhat more elegant than the one we use in Italy to indicate simulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, when you were forming your opinion in this report in November 15th, 1996, what documents and reports did you review before forming your opinion?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I examined -- I would prefer, incidentally to look back at my report, which is printed in Italian, just to make sure that I am precise on this. But I received a copy of the questioning of the accused in July, 1996. And then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me, when you say a copy of the questioning, that was the office of the Prosecution's questioning of the accused?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. I must say I don't have the documents with me, but I think that these were the minutes where we had the Prosecutor -- I am not sure what his name was Niemann, could it have been?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Bart D'Hooge and Teresa McHenry.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Then I got a copy of the three previous reports which were prepared in November, 1996, the one from the psychologist, Dr. De Man, one produced by professor Logan, who carried out this in October, 1996, and Dr. Van Leuween, who did his report in November 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And those prior reports, we're looking to the issue of his compatibility with detention; is that right? They weren't dealing with competency to stand trial?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, it was focused on the compatibility to be incarcerated. Dr. Roorda and Dr. Van Leuween, suggested that an expertise needed to be carried out on responsibility in the light of the clinical data that had been highlight.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you rely on the clinical data provided by Dr. Roorda de Man at that time also?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I took account of this. I took account of the report produced by Dr. Roorda de Man. And I pointed out that there were a number of psychological tests, which she carried out. Some of these tests, quite honestly, things which I am not familiar with, so I wasn't able to compare my experience with the results of these tests. The other tests are ones which are currently used for psychological and psychiatric testing, so there I was able to take into account the data. I didn't get a copy of the minutes or the protocol of the test, rather, I just saw the results which actually mentioned in the report. The protocols are the answers that are provided, the calculations, all the data sheets, which I use during the test and which normally are appended to the psychiatric report. I just got the report from the psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And going to the test that she performed that you didn't know what they were, if a psychiatrist or a psychologist from Italy were asked if why they didn't know the Perdue Peg Test, can you give an explanation for that, the Perdue Peg Test?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: There are tests which are carried out throughout the world, I would say, tests which are then applied by habit in the different countries. And then there are personal choices which applied by various administrations. One can say that at least, theoretically, that it would be advisable that any expertise that is carried out, that one would carry out all the tests carried out in the world, neurological, laboratory test and the like, everything. Obviously, each country has its own traditions. What I can tell you, though, is that Dr. Roorda de Man carried out this, the peg test, and I am not familiar with it. And on the basis of my experience in Italy, I have never seen such a test administered. I have never been asked to administer such a test, either by a neurologist, or a psychiatrist. And even in outpatient care for medical psychiatric patients, we have never used a test of this nature, so I don't know it. As for the other tests, basically they're the standard tests, the Rorschach test, memory scale test, visibility test or visual memory tests, sorry, I should have said and these produced the results that you have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you check the Kaplan and Sadock book to see if the Purdue test was even mentioned in neurological testing?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at the chapter on Kaplan, Sadock, that's what the interpreter heard, and I didn't find that test. But I would like to point out that this doesn't mean to say that this is an invalid test. That is to say, it's not intrinsically not valid. Each one of us can use particular tests because we may feel that it is advisable to see a specific aspect which that particular test will highlight, but it doesn't mean to say necessarily that these tests will necessarily have to be ritualised in a different case. Each one of us will identify the tests that we want to use and we tend to use the same tests over and over again. There are certain cases of violent criminals. For example, it may be useful -- and in Italy we use this, the Rosenzweig test, which is a test that looks at the frustration tolerance level of the individual to see what the trigger point, what is the coefficient that will lead to a reaction of an individual, when there are crimes triggered by an activity of the victim. For example, everybody knows you've got the classical case of homicide, where the victim will tend to say, shoot me if you have a courage to do so. In such cases, it is useful to use the Rosenzweig test to see the frustration tolerance level of the individual. The Rosenzweig test is not widely used, at least not in many other cases. We wouldn't use it ourselves, for example, in a case of somebody trying to hide senile dementia. I am not familiar with the test and I must say, if you would allow me to do so, that all the other psychiatrists whom I have spoken to don't know it either. And in my day-to-day work, I have never been asked to carry it out, but that doesn't mean to say that it is a bad test.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you're the one who -- did you look at Dr. Roorda de Man's psychological testing and did you determine that they were incomplete and that we needed to have been Landzo psychologically tested again?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Now, I have been able to observe that Dr. Roorda de Man and Dr. Verde, in fact, answered these questions yesterday, but she came up with some very partial answers to some of the tests, particularly to the Rorschach test and these examinations were carried out some two years ago. So I thought it might be appropriate to ask that a new examination be conducted, that is a psycho-diagnostic examination of Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It was clear from Dr. Roorda de Man's report, that the fact that she was unable to give any projective testing results was not due to her, it was due to a problem with Mr. Landzo's responses; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I would say yes. You have to bear in mind that every psychiatric diagnosis in a psychological evaluation, even when you're administering tests, will really derive from a relationship from two persons. So it's also possible that the answers to a particular test may be influenced, either because of the cooperation that exists of the person being examined, or by other factors. So I thought it was necessary to ask for a new examination to be carried out, so that we could have comparative data with which to contrast the earlier data.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In your opinion, could those tests in 1996 been influenced by the PTSD disorder?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: The post-traumatic stress disorder was the evaluation made by my colleague, so I would say yes. I think that to a certain extent, the test did confirm this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like for you to look at your first report, also. And I want to refer to a few passages in it that describe some things that Mr. Landzo told you. And then I want you to relate them, if you can, to his mental disorder that you have discovered. Now, one is --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: May I ask you the page you're quoting from, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am starting on page 16, right now. And, Your Honours, I will provide the Court with copies of these at the break. Where he talks about throwing a hand grenade into an apartment where some young girls were there and holding them in there for two hours and not allowing them out. Or where he says -- sorry. Or where he says things like, "I would have killed my father too, if he had appeared in front of me as the enemy." Or where he says that he preferred close-range fighting to a good lunch. Or where he says he remembers seeing people being beaten and injured and he remembers how somehow that seemed normal because in war one learns not to see others as human beings, but as animals that are always potentially dangerous. And I am sure this report has other examples of this kind of description. Can you relate these to the personality disorders that you have found?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, to do that, I will have to introduce the discussion on the diagnosis, but in order to do so, I must, indeed, inform the Court about a number of points contained in my second and my third report. So you're asking me to anticipate here by conclusive statement in the diagnosis and then go back to the first report and explain what's in the first report which I drew up. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I apologise for my lack of organisation in this. Your presentation and your idea of how it should go is much more organised than mine, so I defer to you. It's just a little painful to read these out again, but I will later on, so -- let's go on to your second report.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I'll try and explain this point to the Court, if I may. I carried out an examination on three occasions over a year and a half of the accused. My colleagues, who worked independently, and myself, we have reached a different sort of understanding. We first saw just on post-traumatic stress disorder, and we had, indeed, understood some personality aspects of that person concerned. We then were able to better understand other aspects of his personality, a dependent personality with a narcissistic component. And in my third report, I have reconsidered, reread what had been covered earlier on. So, I would like to qualify this by saying that the diagnosis I have come up with, was, indeed, the result of a number of points that we gradually understood. So let me try and speak in my personal capacity and tell you what my position is. When I did write the sentences that were quoted by the attorney for the Defence, I did write these sentences, because I felt that these were points that are related to a personality which was rather fragile, relating the post-traumatic stress disorder condition. With the present understanding and knowledge that we have of Mr. Landzo, I can now express a view which indicates that what he has stated can be more related to his dependent personality and an attitude that he has at acting out a specific role, rather than simply being related the post-traumatic stress disorder. So I would say that the sentences you have quoted could be construed as being related, to some extent, to the post-traumatic stress disorder, but, more importantly, they can be related to the acting out attitude that he has in his own personality. It's inherent in his personality. It takes on this role as he has a dependant personality. And I would like to give to the Court a very clear example of that. In my report, in my third report, I have quoted Woody Allen's movie, Zelig, where the leading character, when he was in touch with the given person, he would, indeed, step in that person's shoes and will become that person himself. And that's the whole beauty of the movie itself. And so I could read it and construe these sentences as being an indication of the person that, indeed, acts out the role of an aggressive -- perfect aggressive soldier and fighter. And that was the role that Mr. Landzo, indeed, has taken on whilst he served in the armed forces. When we met him in 1996, he still retained such a role. So I would say that these views expressed about his role are consistent to the fact that he was a sort of a taking on the role of a fighter, a mercenary that loves to fight and loves to kill the enemy. At a later stage, Mr. Landzo gave a different interpretation of the same sentences that he uttered on those occasions and today has a completely different position. So apparently, today we're faced with a person that seems to be quite different from the one that we met at first in 1996. So in terms of the psychiatric evaluation, which I have given, I would say that the present attitude that Mr. Landzo has must be interpreted simply as a new type of attitude which he has taken on, which is consistent with his dependant personality, which is basically inspired by the -- by his reference to a dominant authority. Back in 1996, when we first met him, the military frame of reference was a dominant frame of reference at that time, so he would emphasise this attitude at that point in time. Whilst, today, he shows us a different attitude which is excessively consistent with the role of an ideal prisoner, detainee, that is, indeed, involved in his own defence. But this speaks to his incompetence and inadequacy. And it is on the basis of his inadequacy that we, indeed, have come up with the definition of a major personality disorder that he suffers from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, I want to go back to your first meeting with Mr. Landzo in 1996. I am going to describe -- well, I am going to let you describe him. Did he have his head shaved then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What relevance does that have in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it identifies him with the military thing. And I have to bring that up before the Court that he wore camouflage clothes, he wore a cap with the skull and cross bones on it and who he was able to visit with in 1996 and versus who he is able to talk to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How does that go to diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It verifies the DSM IV, personality disorder pathology of dependant personality and mixed personality that every one of these psychiatrists is going to talk about. If you'll allow me, it's only a couple of questions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you remember in 1996 that he was only allowed to talk to one or two other people that he was detained with?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that he hated the Serbs, he hated the Dutch. So on the one hand, he did say that he hated almost everyone. On the other hand, he had a sort of avoidance behaviour with respect to recalling such events because he said if he were asked to recall this, this made him suffer and it made him think about the war. So this is one of the many inconsistent behaviours that he showed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just want find out, if you know, can you describe his appearance that you saw in 1996 and also, do you know, if you know, whether he was allowed to talk to other people or not, without mentioning any names?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I don't recall this particular point. But as far as I can recall, he was not allowed to talk to the other accused. He could talk to some other people, though. But I feel he did have the same problem with the guards as well, guards that were coming from former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you don't determine in your evaluations whether the subject is telling the truth or not, do you? Explain that to the Court, what it is you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: This brings me to a far lengthier presentation than I need to make and I'll try and be as brief as possible, not to take too much of the court's time. In any psychiatric evaluation, one has to consider two levels of examination. First, a clinical level, that is the medical, psychological level of evaluation, which is conducive to a diagnosis. And the second level is how we can incorporate such a level into a legal dimension that is referring back to a legal provision or a legal definition. Now, it's quite obvious that if a legal expert -- psychiatric expert, sorry, does have a frame of reference, which is specific concerning the events on which a trial is being carried out, then the expert, the psychiatric expert is in a better position to understand the consistency of statements made by the person who is interviewed and the facts which are being attributed to that person. If not, the truthfulness of his statements in my three evaluation, I would say, I could only take Mr. Landzo's words as a point of reference. And this an is a very major limitation in methodological terms. I could compare what he said to the results of tests which were administered by Dr. de Man. In the last report that I wrote, I could build on the results of Dr. Verde's test as well. As a medical doctor and as a specialist, I can recognise a major gross simulation, malingering, as the one carried out by Mr. Landzo, but I cannot tell whether or not he is telling the truth. And I must assume that he is expressing his own subjective truth, what, in psychiatric term, is defined as his own perception or one's own behaviour. So his perception of his life experience, as it were. So we must, indeed, acknowledge that this is a major limitation to this type of expertise, of expert evaluation. So both myself and Dr. Van Leuween did ask to examine the person in a situation where we would be free to discuss the events with him. So, as I said, this is a methodological limitation that we have to consider. So all I can do in psychological terms, is taking into account the emotional level of the person, but I am not in a position to tell what he says is true or not. So it's quite clear that both myself and my colleagues had to base our opinion on what he told us. For instance, what he told us about his own personal history, his relations to his mother and his experiences when he was being trained in that Croatian training camp back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you don't look to the truth of what he says. And I am going to ask a fairly leading question, so that we can get through this material, if you will indulge me. You look to whether the clinical symptom proposed is related to the clinical evidence; would that be a fair statement, and how it applies to a personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. Let's say that the person shows a number of clinical symptoms. These clinical symptoms may be true or not. So we as psychiatrists identify them as true clinical symptoms if they do appear to be related with the general picture of the individual, the tone of the voice, his emotions, so if everything else, seems to be consistent with his attitude. If, instead, the clinical symptoms are not consistent to the clinical evidence that we find, then we say that these are not true symptoms which are not -- therefore, they're not consistent with the clinical evidence. To go back to the example I gave earlier on about malingering, it's quite obvious that when he was pretending to have a total lack of orientation in time and space, when he was doing that, this was not in keeping with the clinical evidence that we had found earlier on. So I did feel at that time this was not really true, so these clinical symptoms were not true symptoms. In forensic psychiatry, we look constantly for consistency between symptoms and evidence in order to identify properly the symptoms. When it comes to the second level of forensic level of evaluation, then it's a far more complicated exercise that we need to carry out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him right away what his findings are with regard to his metal disorder, with regard to his diminished ability. We've heard a lot of theory. But let's come down to straight to the case now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought it was important to see the different levels from '96 and the changes, but I do want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to ask him one that I think is very important to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You don't only base your conclusions on what Mr. Landzo tells you, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If somebody wants to challenge him, he can cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I always try to head off the cross-examination ahead of time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't try to do that. Just get your conclusions and someone wants to find out the reason, he can ask the doctor to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Could he just tell you the three criteria that he looks to when coming to a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him about the conclusions about this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Verde, I am going to jump over to the end and then work backwards. After your three evaluations of Mr. Landzo and the many hours that you've spent with him, would you tell the Trial Chamber what it is that you have concluded today about the personality disorders or the pathology and explain that to the Court that exists in Mr. Landzo now, when he was a child, and that existed in 1992. Is that better, Judge Jan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just be a little more relevant, more pointed. I'm more interested in the conclusions. If somebody wants to challenge his conclusion, he can cross-examine him and the doctor can give all of his explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want him to give the conclusion that it's not a conclusion of just today, it's a conclusion of what he was suffering in '92 and before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let him do it instead of going roundabout it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, is a bottle-line person, like I normally am except when I am presenting my case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, Dr. Lagazzi, would you explain to the Court what it is you found in Mr. Landzo and how it relates to this case.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I can certainly do that. Mr. Landzo does have, at present, a very complex clinical problem. So there are several levels that need to be considered in that clinical picture. The first level, if we take the DSM IV, could be rated as being S1, which is that of post-traumatic stress disorder. I did attach more importance to the post-traumatic stress disorder in my earlier evaluation. In my first and second report was now, I consider this to be of lesser importance, because it's to be considered part and parcel of the more global personality disorder, so it would be rated 2 in DSM IV. And I found there is a major personality disorder with a person that has strong problems of impulsiveness and narcissism. And, psychologically speaking, he appears to be immature, so he has a delayed psychological growth when compared to his actual age. And I consider that these conditions were also to be found back in 1992. And specifically, the time that we are discussing here, when he was at the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, when you say DSM IV, you're not saying that PTSD doesn't exist now, you're just saying that it's part of a much larger personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. In my evaluation, the personality disorder existed at the very outset. It then developed to PS -- PTSD and we found -- we find in the literature a more severe form or PTSD, when you have a dependant personality disorder which is concurrent with it, then there is further development of such disorders, and they're all to be found in his present condition. Then his specific experience has had a bearing on it. His being in the camp. His being in prison in Bosnia at the time. He has spent in detention now. This has developed into very rapid changes in his position vis-à-vis the outer world. So in clinical terms, these are the changes which I have emphasised in my report and which are borne out by the results of test, which were carried out by Dr. Verde.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber understands, this immaturity that you talk about, that's not the sole pathology, and would you tell the Court what pathology means to you in your psychiatric terms?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: We do have a definition of mental disorder in international literature which applies to a stable condition which causes suffering to the person, to the patient and results into poorer self-perception, lesser ability to relate to other people and behavioural difficulties. When we refer to words, such as pathology, or psycho-pathology, in psychiatric terms, this is not a subjective term. Psychiatry has several models that it goes by. The descriptive model, which is DSM, is just one of the models. Both the DSM and the classification, which has been worked on by the World Health Organisation, ECD, go along the lines of descriptive model. Whilst there are other models that apply dynamic psychiatry, as it were, which attribute to the world pathology a more relative meaning in that it is applied to individual patterns of behaviour. And we find one such example on a day-to-day basis in our forensic psychiatric work in behaviours that refer to the sexual behaviour. So if we use the word pathology, the word pathology has a different meaning according to the condition involved and it is taken to mean lack of self-control on the part of the subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, just for a bottom line definition, is your definition of pathology and forensic psychology, does that mean illness or disease?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: The notion of disease, especially related to something that is more limited in -- has a more limited time frame, so we would rather use here the word illness. So there is a difference between what is meant by disorder and what is meant by illness, in that disorder is a term which gives a generic definition of a condition, whilst illness does cover through pathology. This might create problems when I am going to be cross-examined, but I think it's appropriate that I try and define that more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just for clarity purposes, you have a copy of the criteria from Kaplan and Sadock that was introduced into evidence as D 484 before; the criteria, I believe it's in that book on page 776 and 777.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: We have not discussed this bottom line type testimony yet, so -- 776 and 777.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: To make it clear for the Court, would you point out what DSM IV disorders Mr. Landzo absolutely suffers from. You can't use the word absolutely. I take that back. In your opinion, what he suffers from on this table of specific personality disorders. And if you can't explain it through these, then use whatever table you like.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Let me try and explain. Are you referring to Table 27, page 776 of Kaplan? If you're referring to that, that doesn't cover the criteria for DSM IV, but ECD 10, rather, that is the other psychiatric classification. The two have been more or less combined, but in the Kaplan classification, in the next page, you have the DSM IV forms for individual disorders. So we could use the one you mentioned, but this is not for the DSM IV. The criteria are more or less the same, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Since I was incorrect in presenting these to the Court, could we ask the assistance of the usher to turn on the ELMO so we can put the DSM 4 criteria, so that everybody can see it on their monitors?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to ask the counsel to provide the registry with the copies of these pages, because otherwise I will be obliged to keep the book for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You have the page 777 and 776 as D 48/4. But this new one, I will most certainly supply a copy as soon as we have our break in a moment. I would like it clear for the registry, I haven't seen it yet either, so -- yes, would you put that -- can he sit closer to the ELMO so he can use the book at the same time that it's displayed over the ELMO. Your Honours, it may be simpler if we take the break now and I make copies for everybody. Would that be more appropriate? It is 11.30 and I have been standing for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you choose to be relevant in many areas, you have to spend that time, wasting your time. I think we can have the break at 11.30 and come back at noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Saunders is still down at the one Defence copying machine, making copies. So if I might just cover one other area real quickly before he returns, I expect him any moment with those copies. Because I don't have the book to put it on the ELMO because he has it down copying at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lagazzi, you have described pathology as an illness and, would you, please, demonstrate to the Court exactly what a psychiatric illness is based on your definition of pathology.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case, we need to speak of an abnormality of the personality. The term illness is very clear. If you refer to psychiatric pathology, such as the one we describe as being a major problem, such as schizophrenia or delirium or some other thing of that nature or what we call the bipolar disorders, as such, as manic depressives, these are evident pathologies. And these are very clearly definable as illness. If we're talking about a personality disorder, what we're talking about basically is something that is abnormal in the personality of the individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Lagazzi, would you explain with your diagram of what pathology is in a psychiatric disorder situation. I believe we discussed something called the red shoes?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: This is an example that I have used with the Defence and with the Prosecutor as well. I would like just to point out that what we're talking about now is a much less easily defined field than a personality disorder. That is to say, abnormality in the personality. If we're speaking of schizophrenia, for example, it is very clear to everybody concerned that this is always a pathology. That it is always an illness. If we're speaking of a personality disorder, we're speaking of something that is abnormal, so we need to define the term. And we need to say when normality becomes something that spills over into abnormality and becomes a pathological situation. If you want and if I am given the permission to do so, perhaps I could just sketch out something just to demonstrate the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Pathology be concerned with the change in the composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even abnormality, it can be defined, actually as an abnormality in the structure and in the expression of a personality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- in the chemistry of the pain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a very interesting question you asked me. Currently, the field of neurobiology, neurochemistry in psychiatric fields is something that is on an expansionary curve. But we're dealing with a fact. The drugs that we use, either to deal with psychotics or depressives are chemical substances, and which, therefore, have an influence on the chemical nature of an individual and modify behaviour, of course. We are pretty sure of what disorders come from direct cerebral lesions, that is neurological problems. In psychiatric areas, there are studies which show that in certain pathological cases, there is a change in the chemical composition. But if we're speaking of personality disorder, it is very difficult to speak of real changes in the brain chemistry. Basically, what we're talking about in such cases is a model of behaviour or behaviour pattern which develops from the personality. In other words, we've got to look at changes in chemical composition in such cases. But that is something that is very difficult to do at the present time. My personal opinion, though, is that in 100 years time, psychiatry as we know today will be completely different. It will be much more chemistry focused and we will have much better knowledge of how the brain functions. At the present time, we have to resort to the things that we have available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Dr. Lagazzi, before you go into your demonstrations, I would like to know exactly the reference which was made to you, how you relate the disorder to the mental ability of the accused person to commit offences against which he is charged and the extent to which he is responsible. This is what I thought you are here to give your expert opinion about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Well, Your Honour, I must admit that the whole question of responsibility which I have set out in my report is an evaluation based on probability. In other words, we're dealing with an assessment, which is not based on certainty. After all, we're dealing with personality disorders and we're confronted with a person who probably committed certain acts, but of which he hasn't spoken of with me. So, what I have done is to assess the individual and I believe that this kind of personality, in specific circumstances of authority, may lead to the acceptance of an order and lead, in turn, to certain attitudes without using one's free choice. In other words, where free will is absent. But I should point out that the assessment that I made was based on probability and only probability. So I have looked at the clinical data and without being able to know all of the facts, I said what the probability was. In other words, Mr. Landzo had a clinical condition and it was probable on the basis of that condition that when he received very specific orders, that he would then an act in a non-free manner. That was the assessment that I made. And I would just like to repeat that this is an assessment which cannot be based on greater certainty unless you have a free discussion of the facts. And we have to ask Mr. Landzo how he experienced the facts. And this was an exactly the same kind of situation when the question was asked of Dr. Van Leuween. We've had discussions and we've had tests and what we do is to correlate the results, knowing his personality and determine what the behaviour is going to be. But this is always based on probability, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Lagazzi, you also include the third prong of your consideration, which is your own personal observations, not just what Mr. Landzo told you, right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Of course, I based all these aspects on my own personal observations, on my discussions, on the clinical examination and on the results of the test. And I must say that my assessment is also very much in line with the assessment made by my other colleagues, particularly that of Professor Van Leuween. But let me repeat, the reliability coefficient of psychiatric evaluations is greater if you've got more information fed to the psychiatrist, so it's important too the amount of information they're given. So if we were to have a discussion on the facts, we would be able to say on the basis of those facts, Mr. Landzo could have been in a condition of diminished responsibilities and for other circumstances, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, you know, absent the facts, you can rely on collateral investigations in speaking to other people and other sources of information about Mr. Landzo too, right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, if the Court tells us that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think that this will become clearer about a pathology or a disease of the mind if you demonstrate the way you did to me and to the Prosecution about the red shoes.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Obviously this is not a joke, huh?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, this is not a joke.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I just wanted to illustrate this point with an example and it illustrates a kind of behaviour. I want to use this example both with the Defence as well as with the Prosecutor, in order to show how certain types of behaviour in individuals have a pathology threshold which has to be said to be relative. Let us draw a typical graph. And this is very theoretical, of course. Here we have abnormality, the abnormality of an individual's behaviour. Let us just take as an example, one of the borderline cases, so that you can see better what I am trying to talk about. Let us just take sexuality. We an all know that this is relative. And it changes, obviously, very much from one individual to the next. We're talking about paraphilia on the basis of DSM IV and the kind of behaviours which may differ from physiology behaviours. You may deal with a person who is sexually excited at work looking at a woman who puts on red shoes, or black shoes for that matter. Now if we take this as being a case of normality, theoretic normality, it is possible that an individual who has fantasies regarding a beautiful woman who wears a particular type of shoe, these are fantasies which, obviously, will not have an impact on their personal lives or on their work. And it is part of the subjectivity. This is something that is considered part of a normal makeup of an individual. If that person has relations with his wife who wears a particular type of shoes, then we're dealing with less free will in the behaviour of that individual because there is a kind of conditioning that is taking place. And his internal needs are reflected in this manner, but you cannot speak of pathology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What does abnormality represent in this chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, what we are representing is the abnormality coefficient. And on this axis, this is behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Dr. Lagazzi, I believe something is lost in the interpretation. If you don't use red shoes, if you just say any shoes, then it's not as a specific circumstance that triggers this need, so, you know, I think you just said --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is a relationship between abnormality and behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, but we can continue with the red shoes, if you prefer. If we're dealing with just something that is a fantasy which doesn't actually influence peoples' behaviour, from a clearly clinical perspective, we're not in absolute normality, but we all know that there is no such thing as absolute normality in psychiatry, everything is relative. If this person asks his woman to wear shoes of a particular nature when they're together, then his behaviour is somewhat more conditional and it is different from most of the population. If that person is capable of meeting his -- or, having a relationship with his woman only if she's wearing red shoes of this particular type and in all other cases he is impotent and cannot have any sexual activity, then one would say that that person is moving further along the abnormality curve. But we're not in a pathological situation, we're talking about a situation which may be of interest to the clinician and it may be useful for a person to go through pyschotherapy in order to address this problem that he may have. However, if the person in question, in order to satisfy his need to have sexual relations only with woman wearing red shoes and if that person frequents prostitutes who have a particular type of behaviour, then that person is even more conditioned. If the person in question then manages to get hold of a woman, beat her and rape her, just because she's wearing red shoes, then, of course, we're dealing with totally abnormal behaviour and that is, therefore, the abnormality, total abnormality of the personality. What we're speaking is a continuum. We're speaking of a continuum. In other words, we start with things which are present in each one of us. In the case of Mr. Landzo, you have got, obviously dependency, narcissism and so on. And all of these things are present in each one of us. But if you want to define this as pathological, you need to look at gradation. If we take at this level a pathological threshold for the behaviour change, it is obvious that everybody would agree that any person who rapes a woman and putting on -- or, puts on red shoes, obviously, is in a pathological situation. All this has to be plotted against a curve which is a continuum. So we look at behaviour and define pathology on the basis of the degree of conditioning which that behaviour will have on the person in question. If we try and apply this to personality disorders, and this is where DSM IV comes in, we may have characteristic traits which are present in each one of us in a stronger or less strong manner and we wouldn't consider this to be pathological, they're just part of our makeup. However, if these characteristics lead to the structure of a personality which is rigidly defined and guided in a certain manner, then we would speak of abnormality of the personality. When that personality/abnormality is such as to seriously impair the way a person behaves, then we would speak of pathology, a pathology of the personality. So, in this case, and I am repeating the point. It's not as in the case of psychosis, paranoia, schizophrenia, a clear term to work with, we need to look at the disorder and the level of the disorder. If you've got a borderline personality disorder and a structured disorder where the normality threshold, which may be present in one disorder is very limited because we're dealing with a disorder that is very close to psychosis by away of its characteristics. So if we're speaking of a histrionic personality disorder, then the pathology threshold is higher because there are certain manifestations which may be present in a very strong manner and this may affect people who go about their work. So in the case of paedophilia, the pathology will depend on the type of disorder and the type of conditioning which that condition will have on the individual. In the case of sexuality, let us leave aside the red shoes for a moment, which is somewhat funny, perhaps. But if we're speaking of paedophilia, the pathology threshold is much closer to the left. Because so only in real fantasies concerning small children in itself is something that is already pathological even in that level. So the pathological threshold in the case of paedophilia would be placed here. Just the fact that people would have a fantasy, which in other fields would be acceptable, would be indicative of a serious pathology. Now, if we transpose that so the whole principle of responsibility and taking the example of paedophilia still, we can say that if you have an individual who has a paedophilia problem and is, therefore, a pathological situation and if we wants to have a relation with a child who is in the street with his mother, one can assume that his behaviour is conditioned by a personality abnormality. But I think that any forensic psychiatrist would call into question his responsibility because it is obviously an inappropriate behaviour. If you've got a person with the same problem and it does nothing in his own town and he takes a plane and goes on a sex tour in a country where this is allowed and gets rid of his urges there, then that person also has a pathology that the organisation of the behaviour teaches us that very likely this person is fully responsible. In other words, in the case of forensic pathology, we look at whether the behaviour is actually organised. If that same person rapes a woman because she's wearing red shoes or putting red shoes on the women, he does so in a way which shows that he can immediately be arrested. And if that is the case, one would need to see what exactly his behaviours involved. If that person rapes a woman in such a way that he cannot be recognised, changes his car and perhaps carries out the attack against a prostitute because it's easier to kidnap her and he creates an alibi, then that behaviour is much more organised and I think that could, therefore, be considered free will, compared with other types of behaviour. And that is why I think it is necessary if we're going to make an absolute assessment, even in the case of Mr. Landzo, to be able to understand the facts and to be able to discuss those facts with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, those disorders that you have diagnosed for, in your opinion, for Mr. Landzo, he is clearly on the pathological side, above your line, not below it, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, in your third report, you described even another situation which would explain Mr. Landzo's behaviour, which is very short, about the automobile?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Let me just take another example. In the case of Mr. Landzo, what I have observed in the various analysis that we conducted, a change, a change in versions, change in the way he expresses himself. Indeed, in the first examination we conducted, he was obviously play acting. In the latest of one, he introduced a series of facts in order to minimise his previous experiences. It's as if he wanted to appear totally normal now. So I think it's quite clear that if we're dealing with an intelligent person, and this has been shown in analysis, the person is aware of the trial, the indictments made against him and I think that he is basically involved in something that is self-mutilating. He has constantly changed his behaviour and this is probably due to the personality disorders he suffers from. For example, if somebody drives a car very fast and destroys the car in an accident and immediately gets out of the car, takes another car and does exactly the same thing over and over again, that is a self-mutilating type of behaviour. If it is conducted by or done by a person who is mentally retarded or seriously retarded, then you can explain it. But if it is done by somebody who is reasonably intelligent and is aware of the risk and of the situation, one has to assume that there is an abnormality pathology of the personality, which is conditioned by the personality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Lagazzi, I think you can sit down now. And that example of the car is what you used in your third report. Just so I don't forget, Your Honours, at this point I would like to ask Dr. Lagazzi, you made a first report on November 15, 1996; a second January 9th, 1997; and a third report on July 3rd, 1998. And in these reports you stated your opinions based upon your evaluations, the psychological testing and your observations of Mr. Landzo. And you still believe that these opinions are accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have these three reports entered into evidence at this point, please. I'm sorry, this is the November 11th report, we didn't have a stapler or paper clips.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first report has been marked D 63/4; the second one is D 62/4 and the third one -- sorry, no, sorry, the first one is D 61/4, the second one D 62/4 and the third one D 63/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These reports are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, what we were trying to go into before the last break, I do have the correct copies of the criteria that should be used with DSM IV. And I would like to offer these to the registrar first. That's it. Oh, it's already been marked. Okay, thank you. If you could distribute these to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 791 has been marked D 58/4. And the page 619 is D 59/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you have a copy of that or do you have the book in front of you? Okay, great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have a copy, we sure would appreciate it, just so we could follow along.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
