utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you have the DSM IV book in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I would like -- she's been introducing stuff out of various books and I would like to know what I am dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is probably enough copies, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this is the same document previously identified as D 48/4, then we have it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think there is an additional page on 791 that was not marked in D 48/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Then we do not have that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you have the Kaplan and Sadock book?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just to have a label for Mr. Landzo's personality disorder, I would like for you to explain to the Court or show the Court what personality disorder in a pathological sense he suffers from in the DSM IV?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I take it you have copies of this document. In terms of the DSM IV, we have recognised the following points: A post-traumatic stress disorder. And, in our hands, this condition was brought about by his experience in the training camp, paramilitary training camp. And in our last interview, we understood from that what Mr. Landzo said, and he showed us a film showing that he had an experience that was even worse than that of a training camp. So this post-traumatic stress syndrome was caused also by the images of destruction of his own land and killings, which had been perpetrated. The other major element had to do with a dependant personality disorder. The criteria which are set out here are the ones which are applied normally on a routine basis by psychiatrists. And these are criteria that I go along with, of course. But I would like to qualify what I said as follows: There is something which is of great significance in the way in which DSM IV is being used. It's easy to use labels in psychiatry to get to a common understanding of what is involved. But the fact that the DSM IV is used for forensic purposes has to be done with great care. And this is being pointed out by the authors of the book itself. We have in clinical terms, a multi-access diagnosis, as it were, and that the person shows several traits. He has a clearly symptoms of a post-traumatic stress disorder and he has a dependant personality disorder. In addition to that, he has this impulsive behaviour and narcissistic behaviour. And, as professor Van Leuween pointed out, and I would agree with his diagnosis, you also find schizoid traits present in that person. So over and above the kind of labels that we could use for that case, we'll have to think in terms of a complex personality picture. As is true in every mixed personality disorder, we would rather refer to a complex picture which has a number of components that speak to that complex picture. So they're very closely interrelated. So it's appropriate that we use the DSM IV as a frame of reference. Having said that, of course, each and every trait is closely related and influenced by the other traits. It is written in the literature that the post-traumatic stress disorder, in some respects, is enhanced by the fact that you have a dependent personality condition. And by the same token, if you have a dependent personality, some will be pertaining to the post-traumatic stress disorder of being enhanced. If you add to that the narcissistic trait and the self-ego, which is added up to that, that enhances the condition. So clinically speaking, you have to come up with a suitable and overall comprehensive evaluation of that person in light of all of these points.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, I think Judge Jan has some labels we can deal with. And the labels that you have described that Mr. Landzo passed that graph on the pathological scale as far as abnormality. I don't know if I was clear. Tell me if I was clear?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: It was very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some testimony that appeared in the courtroom yesterday. You are aware that there was a witness here yesterday named Elmir Hadzajlic, known as Miro. And Miro had stated to the Court that he had tried to get Mr. Landzo to stay, but Mr. Landzo left and joined the TO. Can you explain to the Court how this is not inconsistent with the personality disorder that you have described to the Court?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: If we take as a fact, Mr. Landzo's refusal to stay with Mr. Miro, all I can give you in this respect is an explanation based on my perception of facts. I may assume that this could be explained, and this is my personal view on it, this may be explained by the fact that Mr. Landzo felt this need to identify with a strong structure, stronger than the dependency he had visiting Mr. Miro. That is a possible explanation, but it's the way I can interpret this, my personal view of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the stronger influence or force or structure, as you call it, also had to do, maybe, with the fact that his father and his brother told him that he had to join the TO and defend his town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, this is an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're just putting a hypothetical situation, and one hypothetical situation may lead to one conclusion and another one to another conclusion, so let's not make --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will retract that hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The truth is, Dr. Lagazzi, you don't know what other stronger force or if there was another influence on him, you're just assuming based on this new opinion?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I take into account the way in which Mr. Landzo described his feelings vis-à-vis wearing a uniform, his being attracted by weapons and the fact that it is quite clear that dependent personalities, when there is a strong level of dependency, you wish to relate to a strong structure, such as a military structure and this has a considerable appeal to dependent personalities. Mr. Landzo reminded me of young boys that would come to me, and before they were trained for the Italian Army, they would be asked to be sent to the UN troops in fighting areas. We had a great many misgivings about their requests. And when we assessed these young recruits in psychiatric terms, we found that all of them had severe psychiatric disorders, so we would not accept their request.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you also -- I want to take the examples that I read out of his first report on November 15th, 1996 and relate them to his diagnoses. Can you relate that behaviour and those expressions of Mr. Landzo in 1996 to these disorders? Are they consistent or are they inconsistent?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: In the 1996 report, we stated that the behavioural pattern of Mr. Landzo and his personality was very much consistent with his earlier behaviour, which then at a later stage changed radically. As I said earlier on, he really appeared as if he enjoyed being a mercenary fighter. And this is very much in line with the fact that there is a strong dependency on a specific model. But I would like to explain that this is further confirmed that what he stated, "I want to be the ideal soldier, a perfect soldier." So the image you have of the perfect soldier, other than what an ideal soldier should really be. Basically what he was telling us, is his view of viewing a perfect soldier and how he assumed a perfect soldier would behave. That he would hate each and every person and he would act the way he acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you described this kind of disorder in terms of a false self. Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: False self or ideal self?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: False self is a false self.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I said false self or ideal self?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a very elegant question. Let's say that in this particular case, it is more of a false self situation, which is consistent with the level of dependency on another person, which is comparatively archaic, low in terms of development. The ideal self here, would have been the true good soldier attitude. But in this particular case, he has adopted a false self approach. And was inspired, not so much by the ideal soldier type, but he was inspired by some examples that were close to him. So here we shouldn't refer to an ideal self. We are talking in terms of narcissistic approach. So it would be correct to speak in terms of false self.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have a tendency towards narcissism, when I said ideal self.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a very stimulating question, a very challenging one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to ask you on the false self, does the person create this false self because there is a void inside?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. That makes the false self different from the ideal self. Here, we have this very strong feeling of void, a vacuum on the part which is perceived by the person on which you have this overlapping narcissistic approach and at a later stage, you have also this dependent personality trait that comes in. I gave you the example of Woody Allen's film, Zelig and as a result of this, you try and follow the example of a person that has full authority without a critical attitude, you perceive a number of personality traits of your model and you try and imitate your model. This is a far more less sophisticated approach than the one that would, for instance, would be followed by a person that would be inspired to become a priest or to take up a military career. You do have the same approach in that you take as a model a strong structure as a reference model. But this is a far more advanced way of modelling your behaviour on somebody else's behaviour and it has this ideal component, whilst here we have a far less sophisticated and a more archaic type of approach when it comes to following, imitating a model.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And that empty false self that you've talked about cannot exercise his free will when he has to follow -- in order to become his false self, which is totally different from Judge Jan who is looking for his ideal self, I suppose. They can lead, they don't have to follow, the ideal self?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Here the problem of the false self in a condition of dependency is such that if the source of dependency, the person you're dependent on, gives you an order or shows you a specific model, pattern of behaviour, you go along with the order, you execute the order without discussing it. So there is no free will in this respect, which is involved. But let me qualify what I am saying by stating that the free will consideration has got to be taken into account in terms of general probability with respect to what happened this Celebici. Then if he were willing to discuss with me about these facts, then we would have to consider for each and every behaviour what has triggered that behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, based on your psychiatric, forensic psychiatric conclusions today, based on the diagnosis that you have reached about Mr. Landzo, can you project back that in all probability, Mr. Landzo was suffering from an abnormality of the mind in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, because the development of this abnormality of the personality had taken place earlier than '92.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And then did this abnormality of the mind influence his inability or ability to control his behaviour in the setting as a guard in Celebici in 1992 from the forensic psychiatric point of view?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: With the qualifications which I have already given, I think I may say that in general, with respect to that particular period in time, there is a probability that it did influence his behaviour. But we would have to go into discussion with the individual facts with him in order to give a more considered opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Based on the psychiatric -- forensic psychiatric diagnoses that you have found in him, excluding the facts at Celebici, and projecting back, he still suffered from this lack of free will in 1992 and before that and today?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I can tell you that this lack of free will was, in all likelihood, to be found at the time he was in Celebici because of an earlier pathological personality disorder he suffered as a result of the post-traumatic stress disorder and because of the very special relational situation that he ascribed. At first, there was a personality disorder that he suffered from, but I am not in a position, however, to say whether or not he had a free will at an earlier stage that he could exercise. As to the present situation he is in, my assessment did not refer to his free will. If I recall correctly, the notion of free will and responsibility are solely related to the fact that crimes had been committed, so as far as I have been told, he had not committed any crimes prior to 1992. Nor am I aware of crimes that he had committed now. If you're asking me if he can stand trial, I can answer, yes, he can stand trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you that. I am going to ask you, based on your evaluation of Mr. Landzo, what is your projection and warning about the future if he doesn't have psychiatric help?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Let me repeat, that for any further evaluation and assessment on my part, I have a need to meet with Mr. Landzo in a specific, well-defined setting. Given his personality characteristics, I think that there are major dangers of his going back to an earlier condition with the risk of events that might occur, similar to the ones that occurred similar to 1996 in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are you referring to that he, in your opinion, would be a high suicide risk in the future after all of this is over?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I pose an objection at this point as to relevancy of that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'll move on. I just thought it might be of interest to the Court. I haven't heard from the Court whether you can answer that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In ethical terms I would rather not answer to this point and I would rather give a medical opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The relevant period in question is the time that he was in Celebici, so anything beyond that time will not be relevant to the position he is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I will pass the witness at this point. In time for lunch. I hope. Well, I can fill the next few minutes if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you're not tired, go on. You may still continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, good, I have many other areas that I wanted to cover earlier, but I cut right to the bottom line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like for you to just discuss your third report, which was the most current, July 3rd, 1998, report, with -- I know you came to the conclusions, but can you explain to the Court the things that you observed when writing this report, especially the absolute contrast in Mr. Landzo that you saw this time versus last time. And I know that the Court heard that through Dr. Van Leuween, but he has a little bit different twist to it, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: In relational, behavioural terms, there is a radical change in 1996, and to some extent in 1997. He was a person that was very severely traumatised and had difficulty relating to the environment. And this led me to consider very closely his dependent personality situation. And, today, he seems to follow a model which is very strong to him, as strong as it was in the past, this military model, but at present he is being modelled along the lines of a judiciary, a prison, an international prison. He has learned English and asked to be sent to jail in the United States for a short period of time. He asked that he be sent to college. So he is now fitting in this international framework, so he has a different relational approach. He seems to be very keen on showing that he has full control of the situation. Is very kind, very welcoming. He almost gives orders to the guards, as it were. So the limited adequacy of this behaviour seems to indicate a condition of abnormality of his personality. So my feeling is that the way he was inadequate in the past is equally true for today. So this apparent change in his behaviour is just one further stage in the development of his personality. But it's not an indication of greater maturity in his personality. He has the same personality, he has taken as a model something different, that is this international structure that he is part of at present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: While given this window of opportunity, would you explain to the Trial Chamber, the consistency with his personality disorder and the changing of his stories every time you went to see him. How each time he would say one thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness. We can now break for lunch. It's one o'clock. We'll resume at 2.30. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Judge Odio-Benito, I am just moving my things, I am not going to talk again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you, Dr. Lagazzi, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examinations for the defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Delalic's Defence has no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Zdravko Mucic has no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have got a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor did you have a good lunch?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I hope the fire scare didn't bother you as much as it might have, the fire that apparently wasn't. I have a few questions I want to ask you, and they're going towards being general questions. Now, we talked for, what, about five minutes, ten minutes, just in general terms? And aside from exchanging pleasantries, I think that's the only time we've ever talked, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did anybody talk to you about your testimony over the lunch break, by the way?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Fine. Let me -- and this may seem like I am jumping around and probably I am on what you talked about, but I am going to try and keep it in some kind of coherent order. First thing is, as I understand it, you're suffering from a lack of third party information, and suffering may be the wrong word, operating under a lack of information and you're forced to rely on what Mr. Landzo told you about his conditions and how he felt and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. And, in particular, if I were to carry out a more complete assessment, I would need to be able to discuss in a freer, more tranquil manner of what happened to Mr. Landzo, just to be able to find out how he felt and how he experienced the things that he might have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, if I were to tell you -- let me back off. Did his lawyer give you access to the autobiography that he spent the last year writing. Your Honour, I refer to it as the "Life and Times of Esad Landzo by Esad Landzo".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's fairly well-known among the Defence that this thing exists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You never saw Esad Landzo by Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did you talk to any of his friends in Konjic or his relatives or his --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would have been helpful, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Perhaps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: But I would have needed to get the Court's approval to be able to go into a more detailed examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You know, for instance, that Dr. Gripon has been to Konjic a couple of times. You've talked to him about that?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with the colleagues I met for the first time on Sunday about the results of my examination, but I haven't had any other information with the exception, unless I am mistaken, of some news about the figure of the mother, who seems to have been the strongest person in the family group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start off with talking about what Esad Landzo is not, okay. You'd agree with me, wouldn't you, doctor, that Esad Landzo's not psychotic, he doesn't see snakes coming out of the wall or hear voices from Mars telling him to do stuff, does he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're talking about hallucinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he doesn't have any psychotic disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Landzo knows right from wrong?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: This presupposes being able to answer at two levels. There is no psychotic disorder, which could have an influence and distort his perception of reality, so he doesn't have hallucinations, and to that extent, from a psychotic, pathological point of view, the point would be yes. But from a psychological point of view, given his current situation, because I think you're talking about the situation as it is currently, I can answer you that he is in a position to stand trial. As to his possibility of distinguishing good from evil from a psychological point of view, currently, as there is no reference to actual crimes that have been committed, it's more philosophical than a clinical question you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Talking nothing about actual crimes, okay, Mr. Landzo told you on one occasion at least, didn't he, that he threw a hand grenade into a house where there were a couple of girls and then shot it up with a machine gun. And on another occasion he admitted to you, didn't he, that he had beaten and kicked some people in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: What I do remember is the event of the hand grenade, which was thrown into an apartment. And then, this was corrected and I was told that he just shot against the ceiling. I think that on the other point, the 1996 report actually refers to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, actually the 1996 report says there were a couple of women in it. And I think your 1998 report says it was a man. It says it was a young man. It's page 6 of the English version of your current report?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, if Esad Landzo admitted on some occasions, he punched or kicked detainees and on another occasion, he hit a detainee because another detainee had complained that first one had stolen his bread, that wouldn't be a crime? That's on page 5 and 6 of the report, Your Honours, English report. If that's not a crime, wouldn't you agree with me that --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I just need to check what I actually wrote in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me you read one of them just right off the top.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. Yes, I think that these really are crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So when you say that he's never admitted to a crime, you're saying he's never admitted to a crime except on some occasions, kicking people or hitting them?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: What I meant to say is that he only referred to certain aspects. We never actually had a discussion about all the facts for which he stands accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then I can, as a lawyer, I can understand very good reasons for that and I am sure, as a part-time judge, you can understand the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to Mr. Moran testifying and offering his opinion to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know in what respect that is. I think he merely referred to what was a crime or not. That's what I remember him to have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is there any evidence that he allegedly committed those crimes, allegedly at the instance of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think there may be some evidence that I don't give credibility to, but I think there has been some evidence during the Prosecution case and the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, I don't understand you to have been putting it forward as a crime, but as to what the expert reported in his own report. This is what you are suggesting. If that was the case, yes, one can admit it. But if it is your own opinion that that was what happened, then definitely, it is not part of the evidence which we can admit for the purposes of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And for the purpose of my cross-examination, the witness testified that Mr. Landzo had not admitted to a crime and I was just suggesting that out of his report, there seem to me to be considered to be an admission to a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's the only condition under which that can be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and that's the only reason it was there. It was the only reason it was offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, doctor, I think we discussed this -- again, very shortly last night -- that under Italian law and the law that I think most of us are familiar with, there are two standards. One is whether someone is competent to stand trial. That is, whether they understand the charges against them and can aid in their defence, know what their lawyer does for them and things like that. And the other standard that one would-- that I have asked you about is whether someone is, for lack of a better word, legally insane. And the standard I think you would use for that would be the same one I would use, that they either do not know right from wrong or cannot import their actions to what is right or wrong. Can we agree on those definitions?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Basically, I would say yes. But I would like to point out that in Italy, we don't use the concept of being able to distinguish good from evil. Italian law uses the notion of reduced ability to understand and the reduced ability to determine one's own -- to self-development or to self-affirmation, I should say. So I don't think you could compare really with the US-based type approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I was using the M'Naghten Rule from England, but that's same as what most of us use in the United States. And you don't have any problem, do you, agreeing with me that Esad Landzo knows right from wrong? He knows that it's wrong to steal. He knows that it's wrong to do other things?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Now, with the psychological characteristics of his personality, which limit that type of assessment on his part, I could say, perhaps, the answer to that is yes, but that only corresponds to his current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You don't know anything at all about his situation in 1992, do you? I'm just seeing what we don't need to talk about?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: No, but as far as his situation in '92, I have already expressed my opinion and I said that because of his personality, pathology, potentially, probably he was not in a position to exercise his own free will. But this could, of course, challenge his ability to distinguish between good and evil over that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's talk about exercise of free will, okay, just for just a second. There is a security guard over in the corner there by the UN flag. You can't see him. He is sitting down. He has got a pistol on his hip. If I took that pistol and put it against your head and gave you another pistol and said shoot Ms. McMurrey, and you did it, would you be operating under free will? Could we agree that you would not --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Probably I would try and get the pistol off you and I would try and shoot at you. It's my free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. But if you shot Ms. McMurrey while I was holding a pistol on you, that would not be free will, would it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he is confusing coercion and duress with free will, and they're not the same thing. I object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you talked about when you first met Mr. Landzo back in 1996. You don't need to go the your notes, this is going to be fairly general stuff. You testified earlier today that his head was shaved and he was wearing a hat, a military style hat. And he said to you that he hated the Serbs and he hated the Dutch. Given the experience in the former Yugoslavia, you might agree, wouldn't you, that it would not be irrational to hate the Serbs if you were a Bosnian? That would be in the realm of normality?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about the Dutch?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: As far as the Dutch are concerned, if I remember things correctly, he had a problem, perhaps, because of the behaviour of the Dutch during the war. I cannot remember that very well. I would have to consult my papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I used the word Srebrenica, would that help you, doctor? If I mentioned the word Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: It may, of course, apply to the attitude of the Dutch at that period, but I would have to look in my papers to see what exactly this was used in context with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Could you give me the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, I couldn't find it in your report. You testified to it orally here. If it's in your report, I haven't found it. I am just talking about what you said on that witness stand.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I remember that he told me that he had problems with the Dutch. So with the Court's permission, can I have a moment just to check and see whether it is in the 1997 report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It could also be due to the fact that the Dutch were exerting authorities so far as he was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Very well could be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My next question would be that is not outside of the realm of reasonable?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. Mr. Moran has not spent as much time at the UN detention centre as I have, and those guards are the nicest guards I have ever seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- by these authorities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he is asking the expert's opinion, I will agree with that. If he is using some kind of hypothetical, I won't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually what he was saying, if I understand him correctly, when the expert testified in chief, he said one of the reasons why he came to some of the conclusions was that Landzo told him that he hated the Dutch and then the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Your memory is very good, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But can I just point out that the attorney couldn't find this reference in my 1996 report because it is referenced on page 7 of the English translation of my 1997 report. It's on the third line where we talk of the Srebrenica massacre and that's why he disputed the intervention of professor Van Leuween because he is a Dutchman and then a little further forward a few lines down, he says that his assessment was that he had nothing against the Italians, but that he hated the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, he said he never had nothing against the Italians, but he kind of admired Benito Mussolini, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And given the fact of Srebrenica, that would not be irrational for a Bosnian Muslim to hate the Dutch as a group, would it?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: That's not logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's not logical, but it's not -- it doesn't show mental illness, does it?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Not necessarily, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, you talked about a test in direct called a Rosenzweig tolerance test?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Rosenzweig is the name of the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you ever do that on Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: No, I didn't administer the test. In the first expertise, Dr. Roorda de Man had carried out a number of tests. In the last expertise, we used the standard test, that is to say, the Rorschach test.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when you were interviewing Mr. Landzo, all the times you interviewed him, as I understand your testimony this morning, you said not just with Landzo, but with all people you interview, you assume that the patient is telling his own subjective truth; is that right, doctor?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, that is the attitude that we use in forensic psychiatry when we're involved in discussions. In other words, we're not investigators, we're not judges or prosecutors. So, we accept the subjective truth and, of course, we compare that with the clinical reality of the individual and we try to take into account other data that are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, in some general terms, you talked about this morning and then we'll get to some more specifics. At some point this morning, Mrs. McMurrey asked you about what she called the red shoe example. And your first reaction was, "Obviously this is not a joke" and then she replied, "No, this is not a joke." One of the examples you used about that was the example of paedophiles. And for lack of a better term, child molesters, and one of the things that you talked about was if somebody molests children in his own town, he calls into question his responsibility. But if he goes on a sex tour in a country where this is accepted, then he is showing that he is responsible. You'd agree with me, wouldn't you, doctor, that paedophilia is not a mental illness? You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: It is paedophilia and in some circumstances it could be a part of a mental psychological situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that the example you were using of paedophiles, they know what they're doing is wrong, don't they?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, in certain cases, particularly forensic psychiatric cases. In Italy, we dispute the capacity to wish something. In other words, a person may understand that what they're doing is wrong, but they're not in a situation to be able to decide whether to do it or not to do. So that may compromise their free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you would disagree that there is nothing that would prohibit paedophiles from refraining from their conduct, from getting help or from seeing that they don't get around young children?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I don't really understand the thrust of your question. You're saying that there is nothing stopping a paedophile from going and getting treatment; is that my -- the point of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That they know what they're doing is wrong and that they could go get treatment for it or they could just stop the conduct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Basically that is true. But in reality, there are many paedophiles who are really dependent on their way of being. They believe that what they do is not really that negative or it's not a crime. But, basically, we can say that there is nothing preventing a paedophile who understands the situation he is in from getting treatment. In fact, that often happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, in Italy, do you take someone who has this paedophilia and doesn't seek treatment and say, "Well, gosh he just, you know, he has got some kind of reduced mental capacity and so that's okay" or do you put them in the penitentiary like we do?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour I am going to object. First of all, what's correct and right in Italy has nothing to do with what's correct and right in this Tribunal. And Mr. Moran, continues to confuse the issue of the M'Naghten Rule in law with insanity and we're not claiming insanity and this court is not determining insanity. And he continues to confuse those two issues and ask this gentleman about irrelevant theories and ideas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, what is the need for the parallel? Why are you trying to bring in the paedophilia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is talking about to reduced mental capacity and this is an example that he used on what's psychopathic and I just wanted to explore that a little bit about reduced mental capacity. If the Court thinks that's unnecessary, I'll move on to something else. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While you were preparing all of your reports, you had access to Dr. Van Leuween's reports, didn't you? Van Leuween, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Well, I prepared my first report and I had discussions as are shown in the report with Dr. Van Leuween. That applies to the 1996 report. Insofar as the 1997 report is concerned, I can't remember whether I discussed this with Dr. Van Leuween or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I am trying to get at --

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but to come back to the 1998 report, I conducted this in a completely autonomous manner and I only met Dr. Van Leuween three days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I am trying to get at is this: There has been a lot of testimony about the supposed death camp where Mr. Landzo saw people -- saw Croats cutting prisoners throats and things like that. And I am trying to get a time frame on when that occurred. In the Dutch doctor's report, it seems to indicate and it doesn't come right out and say, but seems to indicate that he was conscripted for military duty in the -- well, it says conscripted, Your Honours, and hauled up. It's not specific. In the hot months, presumably the summer months of 1991. It says -- the exact wording Your Honours, "This roughly describes his situation when he joined the army as a conscript in 1991. The weather was warm at the time, hence it must have been July or August." And I am trying to nail down if this is the time he went to this supposed Croatian training camp. If you don't know, you don't know, doctor, and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I can save you time just by saying that I referred to the existence of the Croat camp only by listening to the words said by Mr. Landzo. And he said that this happened in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know about what part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Let me just check. But what I can tell you for sure is that he said that when he got word that war had broken out between the Serbs and the Croats, he and a friend decided to run away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- yes, doctor. I am just trying to nail down first half 1991, second half of 1991, middle of '91, end of '91. If he didn't tell you, he didn't tell you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran was it not the same period when he was working for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, doctor -- and this doctor was sitting out in the public gallery when Miro was testifying. Judge, you've asked my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You heard Miro testify? You were sitting out there?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And couldn't have happened after the first half of 1991, could it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object that was not the testimony. He said he could not remember exactly when he came to work for him at all. So I think he is mischaracterising the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, what he really said was, he wasn't sure actually about the particular dates. What he knew, he was with him from 1991, summer, but he wasn't exactly sure when he joined, he left him in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, the testimony on cross was that he went to work there around the second half of 1992 because both -- in fact, I think he said it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you talk about Landzo wanting to take on the role as a perfect soldier; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said that he was inspired by some examples who were close to him that may not have been the ideal soldier.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I did make such a hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's just as reasonable, isn't it, that he thought the perfect soldier was John Wayne or Rambo, from watching the movies?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. It calls for speculation. He certainly doesn't know what movies Mr. Landzo watched or if he saw any in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- were there any heroes in Bosnian history that he has to see the American actors?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I asked that question, I checked with some of my Bosnian friends and found out that both Rambo and John Wayne movies were shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- in terms of Rambo and John Wayne --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: John Wayne is too old for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, you're dating me, I'm sorry, you're making me feel old now. And my wife would be very unhappy to hear you say something like that. If there is a John Wayne movie, she'll be up until three o'clock in the morning watching it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So this idea of becoming a perfect soldier, that was -- you don't know what he was using for the perfect role model?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't know who he was using as a perfect role model. All I can tell you is that he did tell me that he wanted to be a perfect soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what's a perfect soldier, of course, is going to vary -- a person's view of that is going to vary from person to person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you need not bother the doctor on those ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One of the reasons you thought he had a dependent personality was that he felt like he had to identify with a strong structure, stronger than Miro and that he was attracted to the wearing of uniforms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Confirm what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the army just happened to be where he'd go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, where are all these questions leading to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, they're leading to his diagnosis of Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All the factors taken together assisted him to come to the conclusion he did, not one isolated thing. He took so many things into account before he came the that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that, I think your basic hypothesis is that Mr. Landzo is a dependent personality with other things floating around out there like post-traumatic stress disorder, impulsive behaviour and narcissistic behaviour?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Does someone who has a dependent personality is that the same kind of person that would be an inmate in a jail and would point out to the guards, taking the time away from his visits or take control of the situation in the jail? Does that sound like a dependent person to you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that. I would say that a dependent personality is something else. Rather than talking about dependent personality -- what you described is the personality of someone that tries to get special terms or conditions in a specific situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, if he was described as having -- showing a marked tendency to control the situation and was very careful to see that things were properly understood and sometimes criticised the guards pointedly, although always politely, that would not be inconsistent with this kind of dependent personality that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I wouldn't think so, because this personality is a personality that also shows a strong narcissistic component. The model of a dependent personality has got to be combined with the narcissistic component and the focus of this narcissistic attitude is that the focus of attention that you want to be the focus of attention and want to be the protagonist of what is happening. So if you combine the aspects pertaining to dependent personality and a narcissistic personality, you can come up with a behaviour similar to the one like you just indicated. That he would be a dependent personality all in all, but he would try and be in control of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought that dependent personalities lacked self-consciousness and they needed help to begin to carry through tasks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Self-consciousness or self-confidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Self-confidence. Did I say self-consciousness? I apologise. They lack self-confidence and need help to begin and carry through tasks. That is a diagnostic feature on dependent personality disorder in the DSM IV and the English version page 666.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, what you're saying is correct. Yet, at the same time, let me point out that the diagnostic criteria at DSM IV for a dependent personality are five, or more than five out of eight and this dependency feature is not so strong or so evident. You might come up with a person who is dependent and, yet, when he is performing a task that he knows he can perform, then he undertakes to do it perfectly so that he is gratified and gratifies the person he is dependent upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's start off with those eight characteristics. Did you find that Esad Landzo has difficulty making everyday decisions without an excessive amount of advice or reassurance from others? I would suggest to you, doctor, that a man who is in charge of his own defence in a major criminal case, probably doesn't have difficulty making everyday decisions without an excessive amount of advice and reassurance from others. And I would suggest to you, doctor, that criteria two, needs others to assume responsibility for most major areas of his or her life. The way you described Esad Landzo and in your latest report about how he takes control of situations, that isn't somebody who needs others to assume responsibility, is it, doctor?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I would like to point out that all such features are to be found in Mr. Landzo's personality because of his specific dependent personality, then they might be combined with the narcissistic aspect. All the criteria set out in DSM IV are correct. But we're talking about the same person, so we're talking about the fact that in the same person, you could come up with elements which appear in the same person in a more or less marked manner. Just to give you some example. Criteria No. 1, difficulty in making everyday decisions without reassurance on the part of other people. We do have this image of a person that needs to be reassured and that is a fact that is true. If we do translate that into the narcissistic aspect, which is also present in Esad Landzo, as indicated in evidence by the test, we could tie in this element to an expression of total dependency on a person. Let me try and explain what I mean. The fact that you need to be reassured by other people is something that belongs to everyday life. But if you're so much dependent upon a person that you have idolised that person, and you have become basically that very person, you feel reassured in your inner self on a day-to-day basis. You don't have to ask for this external reassurance, so this criteria is met and is to be found in Mr. Landzo. And I could go over the other criteria and I could -- what I said along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, let me be frank. I am confused and here is why I am confused. I look what someone who has a dependent personality disorder is. And I start off if he has trouble making -- difficulty making everyday decisions and he wants others to assume responsible for his life. And then I look at what makes someone a narcissistic personality disorder and I see that this person has a grandiose self-importance. He exaggerates his achievement and talents and expects to be recognised as superior. He is preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited power and success. I don't see how these two go together, doctor. I don't see how someone, at the same time, can think he can't make normal day-to-day decisions and at the same time think -- have such grandiose self-importance or arrogant and haughty behaviours and attitudes or -- you see what I am saying, doctor?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand what you're saying. All I can tell you is that both myself and my colleague, professor Van Leuween, whom you've heard earlier on, have come to this assessment after several examinations and several expertise have been carried out on the same person. And this is a very special case because, as I said earlier on, we have found this dependent personality aspect, which is standing to a pre-existing narcissistic component. So quite right in what you said, in that if we stick to the individual labels and the individual diagnostic criteria in DSM IV taken individually, there are some points that do not seem to tally. If we take these diagnostic criteria, which are objective criteria as indicated by DSM and any psychiatry manual, if we bring together all such elements to try to understand the person rather than writing up a diagnosis on a piece of paper, then we realise that they are integrated and combined. So, at this point, the feature of narcissism, however paradoxical that might sound, it becomes closely tied in with a dependent personality trait, which, in turn, makes Landzo say, "I want to be a perfect soldier." When a person becomes dependent on the jail structure and the structure of this international setting, he is no longer the detainee who is openly dependent, who is asking for the advice of the guards and is complaining or with a cause, but he feels being part and parcel of the structure. So I quite agree with you, this is a very complicated set up, but that is something for which I am sure of in clinical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Landzo doesn't like, does he? He would rather not be in jail, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have been listening for about ten minutes. This is an alarm signal. It really disturbs our concentration. We can't concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought I might have heard it coming from the computer. That little laptop in front of me just went black and it could be -- it may be that someone may have pulled the plug or something accidentally and the thing may have just lost power, I don't know. But the sound seems to have stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you able to discover what is at fault?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The noise seems to have stopped now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for alerting everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Another fire alarm. I am just winding it down, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Esad Landzo doesn't like jail, does he, he would rather be free?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Everyone likes to be free. It's not peculiar to some mental disorder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that Dr. Laggazi has a different explanation for this if you will allow him to answer that question. I think it's very relevant to this Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Claustrophobia or what.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Not claustrophobia and not asthma because my mommy didn't love me either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He wants to be free and to get free, he is willing to do quite a bit to get out of jail, isn't he? Let me give you an example. First time you saw him, or the first couple of times you saw him back in 1996, whether he was successful or not, he was trying to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object he asked the question whether or not Esad Landzo wanted to get out of jail. I think he ought to allow the witness to answer that question first before he goes on to another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought I had an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know the tactics that I am observing now. When the witness has been asked a question, he answers it. And when he answers it, you can continue with any other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I thought I did have an answer, but if I didn't, I would like an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that at this point in time, Mr. Landzo regards the UN jail, not just any jail, as a kind of steppingstone, a steppingstone to then spend some time in prison in the United States, then go to college and possibly settle down in the US. So at this point in time, he certainly has a far less negative perception of a prison than the overwhelming majority of detainees would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, is that view of the future a rational view of the future?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Even in the circumstances? I mean, even in the circumstances, you think it is not a rational view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it's a rational view. There is a -- on his part he grossly underestimates the actual conditions he is in. And he underestimates the criminal implications. The feeling that I have is that, in some respects, he doesn't feel that he is in jail, at least insofar as his behaviour is concerned. My impression is that he feels, and this is my personal view, he feels in some respects the way we feel when we move about in this building with many guards, we need to be escorted, we know we're here because we have a job to carry out. So my feeling is that he perceives himself as being, say a co-protagonist of this, rather than a detainee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Where do you think, or if you know, fine, where would a person like Esad Landzo get the idea that at the end of this trial he was going to go to the United States, spend a little time in a federal prison, go to college and then live happily ever after?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He never told you where he got that idea --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to ask that this line of questioning is totally irrelevant to the events in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While you were testifying on direct -- let's just get down to the diagnosis, go to the heart of the matter. You testified that your first diagnosis was post-traumatic stress disorder caused by the paramilitary training in that Croatian camp, right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did, didn't you say in your report on page 8 that the present examination, your most recent report, finally makes it possible to limit the significance of any PSTD, post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: -- go to the conclusion of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is it possible he was suffering -- or do you have any evidence that he was suffering PTSD in 1992 sufficient to keep him from having a free will, other than what he told you, other than what Esad Landzo told you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Well, the facts that we have are the ones that we were related by the gentleman and it's also based on the assessment I made and the assessment made of my colleagues. And we had the same diagnosis, myself and the colleagues in question. Now, as far as PTSD is concerned, my opinion would be that this was based on an assessment, according to which this was imposed on a pre-existing problem disorder. And it is not the only central factor. In my view, the elements which characterise the entire life of Mr. Landzo are features connected with total dependency and narcissism. And we heard also reference of a personality borderline case, which is a psychodynamic state and this may be useful, but it's not something that I have used in my diagnosis. What I can tell you is that the main features are narcissism and to the dependent personality which are really things that characterise the entire life of the gentleman. On the basis of the facts in '91, we had PTSD grafted upon it. But on the basis of my information, I have gathered my data from clinical examination as well as what Mr. Landzo himself has said. Clearly, if it were shown that there were no training camp, then, obviously, I would have to change the assessment entirely and I would have to try and work out why we observed what we did observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, you have a patient who is incarcerated and potentially facing a long time in jail, right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, it's up to these judges, these three judges, what Esad Landzo's future is. It's not up to either one of us. And you have a man who, in 1996, acted out during examinations in such a way as, at least to appear, to be psychotic and incompetent to stand trial, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you repeat the last bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And incompetent to stand trial.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then a man who, admittedly with psychological help, in 1998 emphasises that he was not mad and said that he never simulated temporal and spatial disorientation. And could that be because in 1996 nobody bought his story and maybe a different story might be more helpful to him now?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I think I need to make one point clear. If I remember well, he admitted that he simulated what he did in our discussions in 1996. That is my recollection. I hope I am not wrong, but I need to look at my last report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it's on page 3, the 1, 2, 3 -- 4th paragraph from the bottom. It starts out, "He is critical."

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, that he is not mad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that, "He at no time simulated, temporal or spatial disorientation, as he had been recommended to do." That could be a translation error.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but can I just check the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I wish you could, because if it's a translation error, we all need the take our pencils out and fix that?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I have the text here of my report. I have got it in Italian here. And I'll read it out. "Expresses criticism regarding the defensive strategy which was originally suggested by his first defence counsel, and he underlines the fact that he is not mad, and in that certain cases he simulated, with the psychiatric examinations, temporal, spatial disorientation because that was what he was advised to do."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So there is a translation error there, doctor. So, basically, he thought it would get him out of jail in 1996 if he tried to show everybody he was nuts, right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: According to what I was told in 1998, that was what he was suggested by his first Defence counsel. But I can't give you any objective data about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that didn't work. You didn't buy that he was nuts, did you? Nobody bought that he was nuts, did they?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. The issue that they were determining at the time, not whether he was nuts, as Mr. Moran is stating, but whether he was competent to stand trial. And there is a big difference there and I would wish you would ask the counsel to stop referring to it as nuts, because that's not any kind of scientific term that this forensic psychiatrist can identify with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually, the question posed in the report of January 9th, 1997, which is D 62/4. Question No. 2 is, "Did the mental health of the accused at the time of the events in the question affect his ability to understand the wrongfulness of his alleged conduct or influence that conduct and if so, to what extent?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He didn't use the word nuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am using shorthand, judge, and if the doctor doesn't like me using that word, he can stop me if he's uncomfortable with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are different degrees of being nuts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly what my objection is here. I would really like to object to the parallels that he's drawn because that request, at the time, of knowing the wrongfulness or the rightfulness of his actions has to do with insanity. It has nothing to do with the issue of diminished mental responsibility, which is a totally different standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's right. Insane did not work in 1997, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. They all stated that they couldn't come to a conclusion because they didn't have the facts in order to determine that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If Ms. McMurrey would like to testify, I would like her to be sworn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reports are in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is going beyond what her defence says, you know what her defence is. And you're going much beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm just pointing out, if there was a previous defence that did not work, and that's what I am asking the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. There was not a previous defence and the only defence ever asserted has been diminished mental responsibility. And if there was a requirement for an evaluation, it is not a defence, so he's confusing the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What she's trying to show is there was no free will and he was subject to be led by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest this, that in 1996, prior counsel was looking at a defence of insanity and, in fact, based on the statements Mr. Landzo has made in 1998, coached, if you would, and that's an unfair word, but encouraged, suggested, and that defence didn't work. Nobody thought that he was insane under whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, aren't you playing the role of a Prosecutor, rather than a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have got a bunch of reports in sitting in front of me, and a defence that someone, and my client's name comes up a whole lot as attached to someone, that someone ordered this man to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moran, we have three reports in front of us, each of them was directed to finding a different mental condition. First, question of compatibility with staying in the detention centre. Second, the question is whether he can stand trial. And it was finally that there is a question of mental responsibility based on diminished responsibility was actually treated as a defence. That was the last that came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, I suppose unless your contention is that all through the period these three separate defences have been taken on, even if you did that, the suggestion is that it has been taken on for different purposes, not for the same defence of diminished mental responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my contention is this: The various things were done, and I am not accusing Mr. McMurrey of anything, but previous things were done in an effort to get Esad Landzo out of jail, acquitted, out of jail because he is incompetent to stand trial and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The way you're introducing it brings a different complexion into the purpose of referring to the three defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Landzo did what was necessary or what he could --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am objecting to Mr. Moran testifying at this point. He is coming to conclusions right now and presenting them to the Court. If he wants to ask the opinion of the expert, that's the proper way to go about this. But if he is going to offer his opinions to the court, then he should be sworn in and take the stand if he's an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought the Court was asking me a question about why I was asking certain questions, and I was responding to it. If I wasn't, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The differences in the conclusions reflect different purposes of the defence, but that makes a different thing from what the Defence is now pleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No question about it, Your Honour. I agree with the Court 100 per cent, that in early -- or first -- in 1996, there was a finding that he was competent to stand trial, not incompetent. And then there was at least an expertise and investigation done to determine whether he was insane under -- which essentially is the M'Naghten Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your Defence, if he exchanges pleas from time to time, how does it help the defence of Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour -- well, first, when you read these reports, it's got my client's name all over it. Second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Evidence against your client? Not sworn testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, we've got a lot of evidence in this court, in this trial, that was not sworn testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Against the accused, against the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was thinking more along the lines of, and I don't want to use the word because it's an Anglo-Saxon word, but it was brought up a lot in the Tadic decision on hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's a statement of the accused. It's not sworn evidence against another accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you working on that basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No. This court has made that real clear that you're not going to hold this against Mr. Delic. I don't know what the next witness is going to testify to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When the next witness comes, you can cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I just want to lay before the Court that at least, at least, one person who has talked to this doctor has a motive to fabricate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So you brought it out that he's been changing his defences, so maybe the statements he is making about the other accused are not reliable because he has already changed it. That point you've already made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I would also suggest that a more reasonable, a much more reasonable -- and I was going to get into that, but I'll just shut it down now, I'll get that through Dr. Gripon, a much more reasonable diagnosis --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Moran is testifying right now. He is telling you about the evidence he tends to put forth. And I just want to say, for clarity purposes, that the third report never comes to any conclusion, whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not the proper way to intervene. I keep saying the same thing. That's why I never said a word because you just walked into it without even waiting for it. It's not the right behaviour. If what counsel is saying is against your interests, it's up to the Trial Chamber to protect that interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will make a submission to the Court that if Mr. Moran will stipulate that all the references to a superior authority are his client, then I'll certainly let him continue in any course of questioning that he would like to and it may be relevant. But unless he is willing to stipulate to that right now, then I don't believe it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, can we hear you, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my first reaction would be that my client's name is typed into one of these reports. Secondly, I am not going to, of course, stipulate that -- I don't feel like being disbarred for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As counsel, even if you're trying to anticipate what is coming here after, the Trial Chamber can do nothing until that evidence is submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I wanted to get through this witness -- I guess I can wait until a later witness, if the Trial Chamber prefers -- various things about Mr. Landzo, including the fact that -- well, I won't go any further. I'll keep Ms. McMurrey off her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As I have kept on saying, these witnesses have been invited to give specific evidence. And whatever cross-examination you should get through this witness is to try to bring your questions within the parameters of the terms of reference for which this witness is here. You don't go outside of that because it will not be relevant for the purposes of eliciting any information from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am eliciting from him, hopefully, one, the quality of his opinion. And, two, what it's based on. And, three, that it is based on, to some great extent, at least, on statements made to him by a person who has a vested interest in the outcome of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you answering for the Court again?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The counsel is not addressing you, he is addressing the Trial Chamber. Now, much of your summary has already been in your questions to the witness. And I think the Trial Chamber will take that into account when they're determining whatever is in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that's fine. And like I said, the Court asked me why I was doing certain things, and I thought I was answering those questions and if I wasn't -- if I wasn't properly answering the Court's questions, I apologise. I thought I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. I think we've heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 4.30 for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please inform the witness he still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, counsel may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Lagazzi.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: It's your testimony that it would have been helpful to you to learn how Mr. Landzo may have committed crimes to arrive at an opinion concerning diminished responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
