utterances.text: And, at this time, you do not know or have any information as to how Mr. Landzo may have committed crimes over a period of time in 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: No, I do not. All I know is what he had indicated concerning specific events, which are the ones covered in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And so isn't it true that without knowing that how he may have committed a crime, or crimes, your opinion as to whether or not he had diminished responsibility for a crime or crimes is theoretical; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I would like to explain that this is an opinion and not a speculation. In other words, it is my assessment based on clinical work done, which points to a general probability. And, by that, I do not mean that Mr. Landzo at the time those facts occurred had diminished responsibility because this would have to be checked against individual events. All I can tell you in my capacity of forensic psychiatrist is that it has substantive probability and this is a general assessment, which would need to be further verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And, in fact, isn't it true, in Italy under your system and your profession --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object, it's irrelevant as to what it is under Italian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am asking the expert who has previously testified as to how he operates as a forensic psychiatrist in his system. And I am asking one question concerning that. And I think it's fully proper cross-examination that counsel brought out in her direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Isn't it true in Italy you work closely with the police, the investigating judge, the investigators, to learn about to how an accused committed a crime to arrive at a decision of whether or not the accused had diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And your last report, dated 3 July 1998, on page 14 in the second to last paragraph, the English version, which begins, "However, as the responsibility of the subject has not yet been established," et cetera, et cetera, that paragraph basically says what I just asked you about; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And that is consistent with your report, dated 9 January 1997, front page dated 15 November 1996, on page 13 of the English translation, paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I can confirm that. I can tell you that the present examination has provided us with additional clinical insight which enable us to come up with an assessment of concrete probability in terms of diminished responsibility. I am talking in my position of neutral expert. So I think this has indeed has been helpful to achieve a better level of understanding. We could only come to a final assessment when we will be in a position to discuss the individual events specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So that if in some point in time you were to learn the specific events or learned how the crimes were committed, you could -- you may, change your opinion; is that correct, as to whether there was any diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I could. I did provide a global assessment with respect to the specific points in time. We'll have to consider the individual events.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: In fact, if you learned about the facts of the case, the facts could, in fact, demonstrate that he exercised complete free will, knowledge of right and wrong and choice?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: This is theoretically possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So that he may have a personality disorder, but that wouldn't mean that he didn't know right from wrong and that he did not have diminished responsibility when he committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the current report I have drawn up is meant to emphasise the findings I have come up with so far. All I can do is talk about the findings that come up so far. We have seen that there is a pathological disorder of the personality. And if we accept the definition of abnormal personality set forth in the provision that you have referred to, this might be integrated as a condition for abnormal personality. And it is on this basis that I have come up with this evaluation. Sorry, I want to elaborate a bit on this point. For instance, you could have a schizophrenic subject. Now, if this schizophrenic person kills a man because he is convinced that this is a kind of a monster that is after him and he has a hallucination, I think everyone would say that he is not responsible for that. Now, if the same person who is schizophrenic wishes to watches a football match and steals the tickets from the ticket office to get into the stadium and watch the football match, well, he may be fully responsible despite his schizophrenic condition. So what I mean is, he does have a personality disorder, which is of a pathological nature, which, in global terms, we could say does have an influence on his free will. If we then look at individual facts, we see to what an extent there are facts which are dependent on this condition and we could clarify that there was a lack of responsibility or there may be facts where he has full responsibility, appears to be fully responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So isn't it true that without knowing the facts, you can't tell if he did a crime because he was obeying orders because he is dependent on somebody, or whether he committed a crime out of sadistic pleasure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You've already answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You've answered. He has already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Okay, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, would you agree, Dr. Lagazzi, that he has been diagnosed as a faucet of the narcissism that we've heard discussed here, that that would mean that he is a manipulator or a user of people, he uses people as a tool, that, I think, is how Dr. Verde described them. Do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would rephrase this. I would use a different form of words. Verde is a psychoanalyst. I am not a psychoanalyst, so he used forms of words, which are psychoanalytic language. I would rather use a psychiatric language, more of a concrete nature, but the meaning is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: He can appear at times very personable, very charming, very friendly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I do not agree on that. The notion of a person being charming, friendly, entails a relationship of empathy between people. In other words, people that do share common acceptance, and just to give you a typically American example, two friends having a whiskey together and they're sharing this kind of relationship. A person who has an antisocial personality disorder might try to be pleasurable, charming and friendly person, but the psychiatrist that relates to him can immediately feel the aggressive attitude underlying this behaviour. Mr. Landzo was extremely kind to us. He was more than ready and available to discuss with us. I never perceived this aggressive behaviour, which is typical of an antisocial person, but nor did I perceive to empathy. Because the sort of problems he has stands in the way of a proper sharing of his self with other people. So he always had this very kind attitude, very correct and very kind. But I never felt to empathy with him because if you wish to share something, you must have a number of things which you share and you're having your inner self. Psycho-pathological problems which stand in the way of this sharing make it impossible. So this is how I felt when I was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, he can still be, at least, I forget the term you used, but at least it was pleasant being with him. You didn't see a sign of aggressive personality in the times you visited with him? Well, in 1996, was there in any difference in how you related to him than in 1998?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, in 1996, he was definitely more anxious. He showed greater suffering and he had greater difficulty in interacting with other people. In the early part of 1997, we still found that he was in this condition, though, with a slight improvement. In 1998, he was apparently changed and that is what I indicated in my report. So we see a different attitude on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, are you aware or did you have information that during the time in question in 1992 he was drinking and taking pills?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: In the first interview I had with him, he did say that in 1992, he was taking pills, alcohol, stimulants. When I interviewed him in 1997, he confirmed that, he said that he would drink. And he said that after a traumatic event, he had seen a truck with some of his friends being destroyed, so he was drunk for a number of days. In 1998, he denied having said that and he simply said that he would -- that he was taking pills and he couldn't give me the names of his pills. Benzyl-Diazepam, I take, just ordinary Benzyl-Diazepam, which I induce hypnosis and induce to go to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: He denied he'd been drinking during the time in question in 1992 at this time?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: He denied that, yes, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, if he had been drinking and taking pills during the time of any criminal activity in 1992, that doesn't excuse criminal activity, does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's a question of law. That is a question of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I believe the doctor can testify, based as a forensic psychiatrist if whether alcohol abuse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He may have the knowledge, I think to a drunk person to do it, have knowledge, but not intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, actually, Mr. Cowles, your question should lead to us his responsibility for his acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, would being under the influence of alcohol and drugs, in your position as a forensic psychiatrist, ever arise to diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That again is a question of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I believe -- I don't want to argue with Your Honour, but I think an expert like this could give an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's a question of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have asked for mental capacity, but not for mental responsibility, so maybe that's what Mr. Cowles is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now I am confused. Rule 67 uses the term "diminished responsibility" and that's what her filing, her legal filings have claimed as a defence is diminished responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As a psychiatrist and a mental health expert, though, we asked about the mental capacity that he had in 1992. Now, he was asked this time to determine mental responsibility, but he said he couldn't without the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Is it your opinion in 1992, Mr. Landzo understood his behaviour, he understood right from wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to again object that that is irrelevant. Right from wrong is not the issue we're dealing with before this Chamber. It's whether he had a diminished capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is diminished capacity?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Diminished responsibility under the definition of the British law, Homicide Act of 1997, which has nothing to do with being able to recognise the M'Naghten Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, I don't think you're right. Let him put his question to him. It's not a question of capacity, it's a question of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, doctor?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Sorry, I found it. Whether I feel that in 1992 Mr. Landzo understood the behaviour he had and he could tell right from wrong. That is the question that you were asking me earlier on. I believe that 1992 is a time on which I have expressed an opinion. It was a general opinion because we haven't -- we have talked about the time he spent in Celebici. And insofar as the time he spent there is concerned, I could say that he had great difficulty in telling right from wrong. If we think in terms of a dependent personality and, as I said, this is an assessment which demands additional evidence, but if we consider a dependent personality of this sort, who has given a specific order and finds that it is his duty to commit a specific act because this is going to be gratifying to someone he is psychologically dependent upon, then his ability to tell right from wrong under such conditions is certainly very limited or non-existent. We would have to refer back to specific facts though, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Which you've never had?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So you believe that this man was incapable of exercising free will over a period of, say, two to three months in the summer of 1992? I mean, was he just a helpless puppet under somebody's influence with asthma?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Sorry, but let me once again go for the logical sequence of work which I have got into. I do have clinical findings to prove a pathological personality disorder. I do have a legal definition, which I have been given, which refers to abnormal personality as possible cause for diminished responsibility. And this has led me to say that if we combine these two elements, we could say that there is a probability that there is diminished responsibility. I can't take this further. To say that he was a helpless puppet might be perfectly true in light of some facts. It could be totally wrong, false, if related to other facts. So the problem I have is that I would have to discuss about these facts with him. So it wouldn't be appropriate on my part to come up with an assessment and an evaluation which go beyond the methodology followed in my expertise, it would be speculation at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Because you don't know the facts of how he could have committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think he said that so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, you still maintain your diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder in Mr. Landzo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, support it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And you do you agree with the criteria set fourth in the DSM IV for post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Isn't it true for a person to have PTSD, that he had to have experienced a stressor, the traumatic event, correct?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: This is the primary criterion. Without a traumatic event there is no PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And the traumatic event Mr. Landzo is allegedly to have undergone is that experience in this Croatian orientation or training camp in 1991?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I have reached this opinion and I am speaking also for my colleagues because we found there were some signs and indications of PTSD. Mr. Landzo told us he had such an experience, so I tied in these two elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And that experience, though, in the camp was watching some videos of people being killed and he claims to have seen people actually killed in the camp, is that right? Is that your understanding of what this experience was?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that the first criteria in the DSM for PTSD, is the traumatic event has to have happened to him or people very close to him, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: But this event that we're talking about that he claims to have traumatised him, he was never in any danger himself, was he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It doesn't matter now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe you're not being slaughtered, would that not been a trauma?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You feel so bad and revolting that it affects your (inaudible), it affects you in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but the problem is whether that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, that's what they say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Judge Jan, could you switch on your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You don't have to ask an expert about it. Look, if you see somebody being killed just in front of you, would you get a trauma?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, of course, anybody would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But the thing has to happen to you. You must be slaughtered first before you can get a trauma, is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because the DSM specifically says that it has to be an actual or threatened death or serious injury or a threat to the physical integrity of self.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's what ordinary human experience teaches us.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, do you know what his reaction was? Can you describe what his reaction was to this alleged event?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: He said that his reaction was one of intense fear. That he experienced terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That answer your first question?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Jan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That answers your first question?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And do you know what he did as a result of this experience, Dr. Lagazzi?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: As a result of this experience -- well, again, in his words, he went back home and then he joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And then subsequent to that, shortly thereafter, he puts himself in a position as a guard voluntarily at a camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Where he is involved in violence?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes. But can I just point out one detail? And this helps me just to flush out a bit what I was saying earlier on. At the last discussion, the accused said that he was enrolled in the army and then he was sent to the camp because younger people with limited motor experience were asked to go to the camp. So I needed to make that qualification regarding the earlier statement I made. I'm sorry if I interrupted you. The other question you asked was whether he could have been involved in violent acts. The answer to that question is, yes. So he went to a camp where he could engage in such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Voluntarily, no one forced him to do that, is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was posted there, not as a voluntary act. He was posted in the camp, that is what the doctor is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: He voluntarily joined the army, to serve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not even sure of that, because there was a draught. He had to report. There was a law there.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: He didn't run away. I don't want to argue with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you for not arguing with me, but this is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Otherwise, doctor, he didn't avoid the wartime experiences later in 1992 as a result of what may have happened in the Croatian orientation camp in 1991, did he?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: On this point you are referring to criterion C of the DSM IV criteria. And this says that the fundamental issue at stake is the stressor situation which is maintained and which is associated with a trauma. And then there is a series of other elements as well that have an effect. Perhaps I should answer in the same way as when he says that he didn't stay with Miro, but, rather, joined the army. If you just take the PTSD alone, I think one could confirm that Criterion C is not upheld regarding, of course, the general premise that you have posited. But the problem is that, in this case, there were ambivalent stimuli. Because, on the one hand, there was a tendency to avoid something. But, on the other hand, because of the narcissistic dependency type of personality, to look for such gratification deriving from the dependency of the army, of the ability to wear a uniform and so on. And, by the same token, there are analogous situations where people who have sustained serious stress and who have had traumatic experiences or very high degrees of stress and then react in the opposite manner to Criterion C. For example, when you have young adolescents who may be beaten or poorly treated and then, in turn, they act in an aggressive manner later on and become violent themselves. So there isn't an avoidance of violence, but, on the contrary, people try to look for that violence. You could also say that there are certain children who are beaten at home who then become violent as adults or become abusers themselves as they get older.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Isn't it true, though, that if you don't have avoidance, you don't have PTSD?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I beg to differ. The DSM indicates these criteria and, of course, these criteria are important. But each criterion has to be read and attached to specific circumstances. So we have a diagnosis on a number of different axes and then we have a descriptive continuum. And everything has to be seen in the light of a global evaluation. And that's how I explain this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, what made Mr. Landzo's traumatic experience so unique? I mean, hundreds of thousands of people experience the same sort of horrors, what made his experience so unique that that now excuses or diminishes his responsibility or free will or whatever terms you want to use for conduct that he later does six months later?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Let me repeat. If we are talking only about PTSD, then, from that perspective, you all know that in forensic psychiatry, PTSD, as such, and I have recently read an article by Croat psychiatrists on the problem and linked with war crimes and this may not automatically represent something which will have an impact on diminished responsibility on not. But it is equally true that if you take into account PTSD and tie it in with the other elements that make up the personality of Mr. Landzo, we can make a more global assessment. And that assessment may allow us to assume diminished responsibility with all the methodological limitations, of course, which should apply and which have already been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You assume the diminished responsibility without knowing the facts?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I have to answer yes. Let me just repeat once again that what I have tried to do is to give you an assessment which takes into account what I believe to be -- I am starting to tire, I was talking about concrete responsibility but actually I meant probability, concrete probability regarding the clinical situation. I think it is clear that to be able to say that somebody is responsible of a particular crime or is not responsible for a different crime, I have got to know what the individual crime in order to be able to determine that I need to I have a long discussion with Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You haven't had that?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I have had discussions, long discussions, as well, but not on this aspect, not dealing with these aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examinations?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is re-examination. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Cowles just asked you about -- I mean, No. C of the post-traumatic stress disorder. PTSD -- I am tired too, excuse me, Your Honours. In 1996, when you interviewed Mr. Landzo -- would you go to page 16 of your first report, if you don't mind. And in the middle paragraph, on page -- oh, I'm sorry, that's the English version, page 16. He says he remembers seeing people beaten and injured and he remembers how this somehow seemed normal because in war, one learns that other human beings are but animals, they're not like people and potentially dangerous. In No. C, doesn't it say, persistent avoidance of stimuli with trauma and numbing of general responsiveness, would this be not exactly what a numbing of general responsiveness is?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And all of these criteria that are listed for DSM IV and PTSD, when they list the criteria, they don't say that they have to fit every one of these criteria. Like in No. C it says, indicated by three or more of the following, but not all seven; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: This is a standard aspect of a DSM. Any disorder will look for the presence of a determinate number of indicators.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moran and Mr. Cowles have both said, well, if you'd known the facts, you would have been able to determine responsibility. But as you've said before, you didn't limit your opinion based strictly on what Mr. Landzo told you, you had other criteria that you used in order to arrive at your ultimate opinion, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I used my clinical observation method. And I used in the diagnostic tests and I also relied on the earlier observations that had been made. So what I did basically was to take account of all these data.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Which is, really, normally, how you form an opinion in your expertise because you don't always have the luxury of talking to the person about what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Basically what we can say is that unless, or if one doesn't speak to the person about what happened, you try and form an opinion which, obviously, is much more limited, much more limited than one could get from a direct discussion. Even in the case of diminished responsibility, I think that this has to be seen in conjunction with concrete facts. So to that extent, if you don't talk about specific facts with a person and not just in order to find out how the person actually experienced these facts, you cannot really understand how or what was the psychiatric state of the person is when he committed a particular act. So my opinion, of course, is an opinion which covers a relatively large period. It deals with questions which involve a number of different types of situations. And it's intended to have been a contribution allowing us to have a better understanding of the case. So it is a broad answer, based on what I consider to be a concrete probability. But, as I said, if we're talking about responsibilities about individual events, I would need to talk to the gentleman about those individual events.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you come up with a diagnosis of a disorder in 1998, you are able to understand that disorder or abnormality of the mind and relate it back to a certain period of time and come up with a probability; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And Mr. Moran had asked you, had intimated that you had discussed with Dr. Gripon, his trips to Bosnia or something like that. You never discussed with Dr. Gripon any interviews or any collateral sources of information that he had, did you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Actually not. I spoke to Dr. Gripon about this. But during the meeting which we had together, we only just referred incidentally to this question of the preponderance of the mother in the family unit, in Mr. Landzo's family. I don't know exactly what are the sources of collateral information. After all, I didn't work with Dr. Gripon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moran also said that in one of your statements you say that he went to the Croatian camp when the weather was warm. And Mr. Moran, or somebody drew the inference that that must be July or August?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a misstatement of the record. That came out of Dr. Van Leuween's report and that's what I said when I read it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I am asking this question as a response to Mr. Moran's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In Italy, which is on the same latitude as -- or, longitude, I don't know which one it is, as Bosnia, there can be warm weather in April and May too, can't there?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I am not a meteorological expert. Obviously that will vary depending on the year in question and the climate. But from what I have seen from television, Bosnia seems to be much colder than the centre and southern part of Italy, so I really can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You talked earlier in response to Mr. Moran about Mr. Landzo's role in the UN Detention Centre. And I want to ask you a set of facts. You know for a fact that he was in Celebici sometime in 1992 and in the military through '94 and he was in prison from '94 to '96 and at the UN Detention Centre from '96 to '98. Do you know that, Dr. Lagazzi?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So would it be safe to say that he is comfortable in that environment and he is basically become institutionalised, as we would say in my country?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Referring to the United Nations Detention Unit, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Or are you talking about the Bosnia prison as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: About since the time he became a young man, from the time he was 19 years old, he's basically been in custody of one sort or another. Does he feel more comfortable in custody or out of custody, would you say?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Well, the gentleman has developed a very good rapport with the United Nations Prison Centre. I cannot say the same for his time in Bosnian prison. Nor do I know how he'd react in a prison of another nation. But I can tell you that in the UN environment, he has managed to find a good basis for developing the behaviour he has developed and I think it he is in line with his subjective situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Moran kept, even though he didn't say the term malingering, he kept referring to and accusing Mr. Landzo of manipulating the system, manipulating you, using ulterior motives for his, you know, for his statements to you. And just to demonstrate to the Court how you're not able to be manipulated, I would like, with the help of the usher, to show Dr. Lagazzi these paintings that he has already seen before -- there is only the three of them -- by Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I object to this line as not being proper re-direct examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, they challenged him about not being able to recognise malingering. This just shows that he recognises this and he stated that these were photographs, portraits made in a malingering setting -- not portraits -- art work, paintings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What does art work have to do with malingering?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would see them, they're made for the purpose of manipulating the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has answered this malingering situation several times, both during examination-in-chief and even in cross-examination. He even has even admitted that to inconsistent statements to satisfy his situation in each case. He is not telling you whether he is so susceptible to being deceived or not, but that was the situation which occurred at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This is just a demonstration that he was not able to be manipulated or fooled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How does that it show that? It doesn't show that. Show him the photographs if you think that paints anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'll lay the predicate first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Lagazzi, did you see this art work by Mr. Landzo? And, if you did, did you recognise it ahead of time as something made in anticipation of trying to manipulate you?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Let me just say that, obviously, with these premises, all I can say is that I have not been manipulated. So the only answer I can give you is no. Obviously from a logical point of view, I can't say that I have been manipulated. However, if I could have a look at the pictures. Can I show them to the Court? These are paintings which I was shown for the first time, I think, on Sunday by the attorney. This is a typical painting for me. And I have seen many similar paintings done in prison by young persons, adults, who take inspiration from a certain culture with heavy metal type of influence, a rock influence, et cetera, and nothing more than that. So this is nothing which can be termed psycho-pathological. I don't have anything to say about this one. Perhaps you can identify under the flag a body, but I can't say more than that. And this shows a similar scene. But again, I would have very little to say about it. It just shows something to do with suicide. It might show a certain disdain for life, but I can't say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But that last one with the scale of justice up above, didn't you say that that was an example of malingering?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: This one, yes. Because let me say that a picture always transmits to the observer a message from the person who has created it. So I think it is quite clear that all this is very much at the conscious level. In fact, it almost seems stereotypical. It is not of a projection of subconscious ideas. It is a kind of attempt to project an image of oneself. An image of one's future, a kind of edict situation. And here, of course, you have justice represented. Referring back to what was said by Dr. Verde yesterday, this is, perhaps, subconscious manipulation, an attempt to describe an image of oneself, which is as positive as possible. But I would like to say that these are my observations, which I made off the cuff and I could have been manipulated in a thousand other manners.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Mr. Moran had described this scene where you work with the Prosecutor's office and you go out and investigate and try to determine whether somebody had a state of insanity or didn't know right from wrong, but what you really did, when you're investigating with the Prosecutor's office, before you get to the court stage, are you trying to find out, to solve the crime to assist them in find finding this person and describing their type of personality that way?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: When you work with the police as a consultant, psychiatric consultant of the police, you work on a case of a serial killer to try and understand when is it that he is going to hit someone on the basis of findings available and try and work out a profile. So you would work with the Prosecutor and the investigators. Or you could also work as an adviser to the Prosecutor in a forensic psychiatric inquiry, which is conducted on behalf of the Prosecutor in order to determine the mental capacity or the insanity of the person. There are more police investigations which we are involved in as well as typically forensic psychiatric investigations, which are carried out on behalf of the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, Esad Landzo, is not antisocial, is he, he doesn't fit under that DSM IV category, does he?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I wouldn't say he is antisocial. There is no evidence of any other behaviour of this nature. It certainly doesn't fit under the criteria of social disorder of the personality. And over and above the labels that one might have for that behaviour, he doesn't appear to be antisocial in the interview. He has different sorts of problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, in your years of evaluating Mr. Landzo, Mr. Cowles had said, oh, he was drinking and taking drugs and trying to explain that as the reason that maybe some crimes were committed at Celebici, but during all this time of your evaluation, he has always denied drinking while on duty in a military setting?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: I'll try and be more accurate in my answer. In my last report I state that he denied having used drugs and taken alcohol. In the report that I wrote back in 1996, he did refer to his being drunk and taking drugs. But he said that he wouldn't do that whilst he was in his service hours. But then in '97, he said he wouldn't drink whilst he was working, but quite often he was drunk for a long period of time. As to the possible influence of drugs and alcohol on his behaviour, I take it you're all aware of that. But, in conjunction with the facts which are alleged to have been committed in 1992, I am not in a position to give any further indication with respect to drugs and alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how the fact that Mr. Landzo has changed his stories and his reality that he conveys to you, how it relates to his personality disorder, to the pathology that you have found?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: All I can say is that I was very much impressed by the fact that right now, Mr. Landzo seems to minimise, downplay, many of the things which he earlier on said were very significant, which is just the reverse of the sort of simulation which is usually gone into by those who wish to bail out of jail, assuming that they're having mental disorders. So I was sort of wondering, and I was wondering why earlier on he was trying to simulate a neurological disorder concerning his state of consciousness, whilst, at this point in time, it seems to minimise these very aspects. Well, on this particular point, I felt that this might indicate his dependent personality. This made me think over this question of a dependent personality because he was trying to minimise importance of such facts. So he now appears to be very strongly involved in the setting he is in, in this international setting and he tends to minimise a number of points that he raised earlier on. And this is very much inconsistent with his dependent personality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lagazzi, there was a lot of talk about him playing the role of a protagonist now, but, in your opinion, that he is just a continuing victim?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: If we are speaking of a person that has severe personality problems and disorders and has gone through a number of experiences in the past, and, more recently, if you consider Mr. Landzo's age, as a medical doctor, just as a forensic psychiatrist, obviously, I have to say that we're faced with a person who is a victim, a victim of a given situation. And, by the same token, there are many others who are to be viewed as victims: Those that have personal background which is dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was he taken advantage of by those people that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not whether it is your last, does it arise from cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it does from Mr. Moran's cross-examination and he asked about Miro. Just one example.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did Miro take advantage of Mr. Landzo and his illness?

utterances.speaker: Marco Laggazi.
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo was working for him and was very strongly committed to that work that he was doing, so it may well be that we're talking about a very young boy who is working full-time, doesn't sleep at home, but he sleeps at work, so you could, indeed, assume that there is a relationship of dependency in that respect, that he would be taken advantage of. It's very difficult to pinpoint this. Where do you draw a line between dependency or taking advantage of a person? So I can't answer to this question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Lagazzi, thank you very much for being here and giving us your whole day and all the time you've evaluated him. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now before we go, I want to find out one thing. Your testimony, and perhaps your conclusion agrees, that the circumstances in which he was, you believe, he suffered diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The limitations I stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you, by that, also suggesting that excuses him from legal responsibility? Does that excuse him from responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not my task here to excuse a person from his or her responsibility. I was asked to form a forensic psychiatric opinion and I answered on the basis of my own findings that if the legal frame of reference is the following: That is, normal personality can, indeed, show diminished responsibility or cannot show diminished responsibility. I said that this person has an abnormal personality and, therefore, might, indeed, create a situation of diminished responsibility. So that is the answer that I could honestly give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, let me tell you why I have asked this question. You know, there are at least two other particulars. There are the psychopathic personalities who are normal persons, as your present subject, who you also regard as abnormal, the earlier category is excused from responsibility and the present category, you have now included enjoys diminished responsibility. Now this is why I am asking whether this diminished responsibility also enjoys that category of being excused from responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On psychopaths, ordinarily, psychopaths, which, according to the DSM have what we define as an antisocial personality disorder, as a rule, psychopaths are not considered as being eligible for diminished responsibility in Italy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any responsibility, not diminished. Now, the semantics of this category is that they are -- responsibility is diminished, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have used this category because this was the one I was being asked to consider, so I have used the same term as a reference term. If we take the condition of the person at hand, I can confirm what I said. If we refer to the so-called psychopaths, to my knowledge and in my experience, in Italy, for instance, in no way do we regard them as being subject to mental insanity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Well, all I wanted to get from you what was your understanding of what diminished responsibility means. Because semantics is responsibility is diminished, it means there is still some element of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this respect, I would certainly say yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just a housekeeping matter to ask the Court. And if the Prosecutor has no objection to it. Tomorrow morning, my children fly 11 hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you have made the proper application and it has been attended to, I don't see any point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am asking to start court an hour late because I have to go to Schipol to sign for the unattended minors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have very capable counsel to sit in for you. But the Court will sit at 10.00 a.m. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 5.55 p.m., to be reconvened on the 16th day of July, 1998, at 10.00 a.m.
